This paper introduces a system-on-chip (SoC) specifically engineered to deliver deterministic real-time performance at ultra-low energy levels. This study examines such chimeras in networks of planar oscillators, where one element in each population acts as a metastable node. These metastable oscillators function as stable active states paired with a slowly accessible resting state, a configuration easily achieved in electronic and chemical systems. We demonstrate two distinct stable chimeric states: in the localized stable-chimeras, one metastable population synchronizes while the other remains asynchronous; conversely, in the exchange-stable chimeras, the metastable populations exchange roles periodically while maintaining a constant average. Additionally, unstable chimeras are identified, where transitions between pre-existing stable-chimeric states occur, enabling the exploration of the parameter space governing these stable-chimeras. In recent years, chimeras—patterns combining synchronized and incoherent dynamics within homogeneous oscillator networks—have attracted significant interest. This phenomenon has been observed in diverse fields, including electronic, chemical, and biological systems. A notable variation is the anti-chimena, a stable chimera pattern where the incoherent population consists exclusively of metastable nodes. However, the existence of anti-chimeras in standard oscillator networks remains theoretically unresolved, despite numerical evidence. This paper investigates the conditions under which anti-chimeras can exist in networks of planar oscillators, where each planar oscillator includes an additional variable representing a metastable node. Our existence proof identifies two distinct types of anti-chimeras, which we categorize based on the nature of the incoherent populations. We analyze specific two-frequency cases, which are also relevant in the context of quasicrystals. Furthermore, we outline a numerical continuation method to extend these existence results to networks with arbitrary even numbers of oscillators per population.

The rotating anti-chimera features a symmetric configuration where one population synchronizes while the other remains incommensurate, with all incoherent nodes rotating around the ring at identical angular velocities. \section{Introduction}
Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable success in both artificial intelligence research and practical applications. A prevalent and effective strategy in RL, particularly for high-dimensional environments, is Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL). This approach employs a learned dynamics model to either directly optimize the policy or approximate it. However, the underlying assumption of MBRL is that the model is accurate; otherwise, the resulting policy will be suboptimal, and quantifying this suboptimality remains difficult. This gap motivates our work.

This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective method for detecting these changes using streaming data, enabling the prediction of KDD Cup99 attack classes and the identification of novel attacks within the N-BaF dataset. Machine learning is favored here due to its balance of interpretability and performance. The core technique involves training an ensemble of classifiers on a static training set, reserving one classifier exclusively for anomaly detection. During operation, the system dynamically switches to a new classifier once an attack pattern is identified, ensuring continuous detection of new threats. Results on both datasets demonstrate that the average classifier achieves performance comparable to the best individual classifier trained on known attack classes, while simultaneously detecting new attacks with a false positive rate of no more than 0.03.

To address the problem of identifying novel attacks, we employ a sparse autoencoder to extract features from incoming data. These features are continuously added to a database of known attacks, allowing for the identification of new attack classes. We evaluate four distinct approaches for recognizing these new attacks, comparing their performance against a naive baseline that simply counts occurrences of unique features in the training set. Our findings indicate that this ensemble-based feature learning method outperforms the naive approach, while maintaining a false positive rate of not exceeding 0.01.

Finally, we trained a classifier on a combined dataset of KDD Cup99 and N-BaF to assess performance on a joint distribution. This classifier was tested on two scenarios: first, predicting N-BaF attacks using only the KDD Cup99 dataset, and second, predicting the same attacks using the ensemble of trained models. We observed that while the ensemble classifier outperformed the robust single classifier, the unified classifier trained on the merged dataset with l2-regularization achieved superior results. Furthermore, this unified classifier with l2-regularization detected new attacks more effectively than the ensemble approach, although it did so with a slightly higher false positive rate. These findings suggest that L2-regularization should be considered a critical component for the future of intrusion detection systems. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of misclassified samples to better understand the specific attack classes that are incorrectly categorized.

Machine learning offers a promising solution for intrusion detection systems, yet new attack classes can emerge at any time, and existing classifiers may fail to identify them. This paper presents an online learning framework that utilizes ensemble classifiers to detect such new attack classes while minimizing false positives. The

In this context, we demonstrate that when phase measurements are conducted on entangled atom-photon systems, the Ramsey sequence generates interference patterns that correspond directly to the photon's quantum state. Specifically, for atomic superposition states, these patterns resemble conventional Ramsey fringes, whereas for photon binary entangled states, they appear as entangled Ramsey (ER) patterns. The ER pattern is defined as the product of the atomic interference pattern and the visibility of the photon's entanglement. Furthermore, we propose a practical application of these entanglement patterns for quantum communication, illustrating how information encoded in entangled photons—using Raman scattering for long-distance transmission—can be decoded by measuring the atom's interference pattern. This approach offers a novel alternative to conventional photodetection methods for extracting encoded information. Additionally, this concept extends to scenarios where atoms are too distant to exhibit joint interference; in these cases, the photon's state can still be reconstructed through Ramsey measurements of the atom. Finally, this letter may facilitate new experimental investigations into quantum interference within atom-photon entangled systems and inspire innovative strategies for long-distance quantum communication. In recent years, rapidly evolving fields like citation and social networks have generated interest in context-aware centrality measures that integrate multiple contexts to offer a more holistic view. However, calculating such centralities remains computationally demanding, often necessitating the use of sampling and approximation techniques to reduce costs. This paper introduces a framework for computing multi-context centrality measures that incorporates statistical bounds on both time and memory usage. We establish theoretical guarantees for both exact and sampled computations and apply our framework to several popular centrality metrics, including degree, eigenvector, PageRank, and Bonhferman. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our approach achieves significant efficiency gains compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to rapidly assess the significance of the derived values through a statistical test framework. Finally, we illustrate the practical utility of this framework by using the statistical test to identify the most influential individuals within a social network context. Introduced by Otte and Sauer in 1990, these pencils can be assembled into a bundle, allowing the application of standard multilinear algebra techniques to standard issues in matrix pencil computation, such as interpolation, inverse problems, and classification. In 2007, Tisseur extended this concept to regular, square matrices, a definition later formalized by Chierchia in 2016 under the term "eigenvalue bundles." These bundles serve as a fundamental framework for modern numerical algorithms dealing with matrix pencils, particularly those based on the QR algorithm. This paper aims to clarify Chierchia's original formulation by elucidating definitions, proving characterizations, and elucidating the link to matrix bundles. Furthermore, we propose a refined definition of eigenvalue bundles that encompasses Chierchia's original version while offering a clearer conceptual grasp. Ultimately, this work seeks to establish a rigorous foundation for eigenvalue bundles.

This result strengthens an earlier finding by den Otter and Steif, which posited that for measure-preserving, zero-degree homogeneous systems defined on $\mathbb{R}^d$, ergodicity could be deduced from topological transitivity. This study investigates the cosmological implications of a confirmed GWB source, specifically addressing two scenarios: a uniform distribution of primordial black holes (PBHs) and the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model. Our results indicate that a steady state of PBHs could explain the NANOGrav data, with the GW amplitude determined by the total fraction of PBHs, $f_{\rm BH}$, and their density profile. The required amplitude of $f_{\rm BH}$ ranges from $10^{-10}$ to $10^{-5}$, contingent on the GW spectral index, which lies between 2.5 and 5. In contrast, the $\Lambda$CDM model predicts negligible amplitudes for both PBH and supermassive black binary (SMBBH) contributions, which are too low to account for the observed data. Consequently, the NANOGrav data necessitate an alternative explanation, such as early Universe inflationary models, which could generate a GW background through bubble collisions during phase transitions. Such models can produce flat spectra and spectral indices greater than 2, and the corresponding bubble nucleation rate can be constrained by the observed GW amplitude. The SMBBH contribution remains viable only if the redshift distribution is heavily concentrated between $z=1$ and $z=3$. Furthermore, the SMBBH scenario requires a higher number of pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) to confirm the hypothesis, as current data are insufficient to robustly constrain models. Finally, we note that stochastic GWs from PBH collisions could also trigger early structure formation, a topic that warrants future research. (MO-MINLP) problems are a critical component of process engineering, where the resulting multi-solution Pareto fronts offer process designers a variety of operation and investment alternatives to select from based on external criteria. However, generating and visualizing these fronts can be challenging. This paper introduces a multi-objective multi-start NLP algorithm designed to efficiently compute the full Pareto front of MO-MINLP problems. The method integrates objectives optimization techniques, self-adaptive filtering, and augmented Lagrangian functions to explore the entire solution space. Additionally, a novel self-adaptive add-on is proposed to identify and record Pareto solutions while avoiding local minima. By employing a user-defined tolerance for inequality constraints, the algorithm respects operational constraints that may artificially segment the solution space, a feature particularly advantageous for generating process flowsheets. The method's efficiency is demonstrated through two case studies: one involving a novel multi-product separator and another utilizing engineering approximations. The latter case illustrates how the algorithm can transform complex multi-product process flowsheets into a set of single-product flowsheets, each representing a potential alternative for design and operation, selected according to multiple criteria. Ultimately, this approach enables users to monitor and control the diversity of solutions and the spread of the obtained Pareto fronts. Finally, the source code is made available to the community to facilitate the replication and extension of the proposed work. To test this hypothesis, we developed a reinforcement learning task that few-shot few-object continual learning (FRLO) agents must execute. We evaluated two few-shot few-object few-task (FSFOFT) conditions under an anti-forgetting regime, where the agent's state of knowledge over time is monitored and utilized in a feedback loop to guide learning and forgetting processes. The first condition involves an agent learning and retaining, across multiple episodes, a sequence of tasks where a task is either repeated or rotated every episode, with each task requiring the agent to distinguish between two objects using one of five cues. The second condition is more dynamic, involving an agent learning and retaining, across multiple episodes, a sequence of tasks where a task is either repeated or rotated within an episode, with each task also requiring the distinction between two objects using one of five cues. An agent successfully navigating the FRLO task exhibits three characteristics: (1) few-shot few-object ability, (2) few-shot few-object few-task ability, and (3) cognitive flexibility. A model that avoids catastrophic forgetting and successfully meets the FRLO task demonstrates all three characteristics. We demonstrate that Backprop Through Time (BPTT) and Evolutionary Gradient Descent (EGD) fail the FRLO task, whereas Successive Backpropagation (SBC) and Successive Evolutionary Gradient Descent (SEGD) do not. However, when an anti-forgetting mechanism is introduced, both SBC and SEGD successfully meet the FRLO task. Our results indicate that avoiding catastrophic forgetting in an evolutionary continuum of learning and forgetting can yield an agent with cognitive flexibility. This agent can distinguish between tasks and objects, flexibly adjust its behavior based on environmental cues, and continuously learn and forget in an anti-forgetting manner. We demonstrate that incorporating anti-forgetting mechanisms into SBC and SEGD can generate an agent that outperforms BPTT and SEGD in the FRLO task. Our findings suggest that cognitive flexibility can emerge from an anti-forgetting mechanism within an anti-forgetting continuum of learning and forgetting. This approach offers a promising alternative to current methods for addressing both catastrophic forgetting and anti-forgetting. Furthermore, our results suggest that cognitive flexibility may emerge from this mechanism and could serve as a foundation for understanding how the brain learns and forgets, as well as how it flexibly adapts to new information. This mirrors the duality proposed by Dr. Yuan's coauthored paper, "Thermodynamics of the Entangled Einstein-Rosen Bridge and the Entangled Black Hole," and aligns with Dr. Yuan's discussion regarding the entropy of the entangled Einstein-Rosen bridge in the preprint, "The temperature of the entangled Einstein-Rosan bridge," by substituting Dr. Yuan's analysis of the black hole with our construction of entangled numbers and operators. We also discuss the potential application of this method in calculating the entropy of various singularities. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the Bell pair exhibits a form of "entangled vacuum" when expressed in entangled numbers and operators. This indicates that even in a vacuum, the interaction of light cones generates information, thereby providing a solution to the information loss paradox. We anticipate that this research will inspire further exploration of the temperature associated with light cones and their contributions to information creation. Our work is also related to a patent titled, "Bell state and its application in quantum gravity," which was published in *Scientific American* in 2021. We are currently preparing a related paper to be submitted to *Physical Review D* for publication. accretion flow around a rapidly spinning black hole can produce a radio transient known as a magnetar-driven jet (MDJ). This MDJ component may exist within the longer-lived gravitational wave (GW) phase, preceding the disk-dominated phase. We investigate the early jet phase of MDJs to assess their detectability. Our models incorporate the early jet evolution to establish initial conditions for subsequent jet development. Utilizing magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations, we examine how a spinning compact object influences jet dynamics. Our findings reveal that a rapidly rotating black hole (spin parameter $\chi_{\rm BH} > 0.5$) significantly extends jet lifetime and stabilizes the jet diameter. Specifically, a jet radius of $R_j = 10^7$ cm persisted for approximately $t \sim 10^4$ s when $\chi_{\rm BH} = 0.9$, compared to just $t \sim 10^3$ s for a non-rotating black hole. This extension of the GW phase provides a crucial window for observing the accretion disk. Furthermore, in this early phase, jet behavior is primarily driven by the Hamiltonian energy of the system, which is more sensitive to the total mass than the specific black hole spin. Consequently, radio observations of MDJs could identify systems with compact objects. We demonstrate that the GW amplitude during this early stage is roughly $10^3$ times weaker than during the merger, yet still potentially detectable by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) observatories. Finally, we show that radio observations can detect the initial jet behavior, such as the jet diameter, even when standard observatories miss the event. This capability offers a method to constrain the accretion disk radius at early times, thereby informing the physics of the merger. Our results indicate that LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA can detect the GW signal for mergers occurring up to $\sim 1$ Gpc, while the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) could extend this range to $\sim 10$ Gpc. The associated radio flux is estimated to be $\sim 10^{30}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$. We conclude that detecting both GW and radio emissions from MDJs offers a unique opportunity to observe the early jet behavior, distinct from the disk-dominated phase. Such observations could significantly advance our understanding of the physics governing the initial stages of compact binary mergers.

Large Hadron Collider (LHC) commenced operations at an energy level twice its design threshold. This article examines the immediate consequences of this unforeseen event, noting that while hadron-collision physics was unalterably launched on a new trajectory, experiments at both particle and photon facilities encountered significant, though not insurmountable, hurdles. For instance, searches for supersymmetry and other high-energy particle physics models faced substantial challenges. At the LHC, these difficulties were compounded by the absence of a comprehensive supersymmetry interpretation framework, leading to divergent conclusions from ATLAS and CMS regarding the status of supersymmetry following Run 1. In contrast, photon-based experiments like HERA, LHCb, and ThreeTracker benefited from increased LHC beam energies, though they faced fewer issues. Conversely, accelerator-free experiments such as IceCube and Pierre Auger faced the challenge of waiting for sufficient cosmic-ray data to emerge from the saturated hadron-interaction models derived from LHC Run 1 data. Ultimately, these examples aim to illustrate the intricate, non-linear, and interdependent nature of scientific research, which cannot be isolated to a single experiment or theoretical model. Furthermore, they highlight the critical role of rapid international collaboration in advancing scientific progress. We conclude by exploring the upcoming LHC Run 3 and beyond, emphasizing that the scientific goals and discoveries initiated in 2015 will only be fully realized through the anticipated upgrades and anticipated beam energies. This work was conducted within the context of the 2016 Frontiers in Particle Physics conference. Extending the theory of self-scaled skew-anti-symmetric (SSAA) methods, we demonstrate that AskSGD possesses global convergence properties. Experimental results indicate that the method converges at a rate comparable to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) while exhibiting a repulsion effect similar to Second-order Skew Gradient Descent (SGD+). Additionally, AskewSGD outperforms Repelled SGD+ across various benchmarks, including MiniMNIST, MNIST, FashionMNIST, FashionMNIST+MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and Wikipedia. to assign compact labels to the vertices of a graph $G$ so that the distance between any two vertices $u$ and $v$ can be deduced from their labels and a third vertex $f$ representing a failed node, provided it is no farther than a certain radius $r$ from both $u$ and $v$. This paper presents a universal construction for $r$-fault-tolerant labeling schemes with logarithmic labels and a constant failure rate. Specifically, given a construction for $(r-1)$-fault-tolerant labels where the distance $d(u,v) \leq K$, we demonstrate that a $r$-fault-tolerant labeling scheme exists where the distance is constrained to $d(u,v) \leq (K+1)^{O(\log n)}$. Leveraging this result, we derive novel labeling schemes with slightly improved label lengths compared to previous schemes where the distance bound is $d(u,v) \leq d(u,v)^{1 - \frac{c}{\log n}}$ for some constant $c > 0$. The proposed schemes operate on undirected graphs with weighted edges, utilizing $O(d(u,v)^{1-c'}) \cdot \log n$-bit labels with a failure rate of $O(1/\log\log n)$, achieving a label length improvement over the best prior scheme. Additionally, we introduce labels with a failure rate of $1/2-O(1/\log n)$ with $O(d(u,v)^{1-c'})$-bit labels, surpassing the previous best failure rate by a constant factor. Furthermore, we present a variant of the first scheme with a failure rate of $1/2-O(1/\log n)$ and $O(d(u,v)^{1-c'}) \cdot \log n$-bit labels, enhancing the failure rate by a constant factor relative to the prior best scheme. Finally, we offer a label-free extension of our primary technique, resulting in constant failure rate $(r-1)$-fault-tolerant hop-diameter labeling with $O(1)$-bit labels and $O(d(u,v))$-bit certificates, improving both hop-diameter and node-failure tolerance by one. Keywords: Distance labeling, fault tolerance, failure rate.

We present a microscopic model of a bosonic cavity mode coupled to an amplifying element, periodic driving of which generates amplifying photons. These photons resonate with the potential driving field modes, resulting in heating. Our analysis derives a nontrivial analytical expression for the heating rate and confirms that the identified heating mechanism is responsible for the observed heating in a driven mechanical amplifier. We propose that the amplifying element serves as an effective tool to investigate the heating behaviors of bosonic quantum modes across various quantum platforms. Additionally, we suggest that the effective dephasing rate can be minimized by utilizing an amplifying element with a sufficiently short lifetime. This research is applicable to both mechanical and photonic cavities. Given the increasing significance of driven quantum modes, the measured heating rate may assist in distinguishing between the heating mechanisms discussed in this study and those identified in prior literature. Finally, the effectiveness of the effective dephasing rate derived from our model could facilitate the realization of driven bosonic qubits featuring long coherence times. Such driven bosonic qubits hold the potential to serve as memory elements for bosonic quantum codes, which are considered promising candidates for fault-tolerant quantum computing. This study examines a novel scenario where time is modeled as a discrete variable within a closed, loop-like spacetime. We first develop a simple numerical scheme to simulate loop geometries, demonstrating that the resulting loop dynamics can be represented as a discrete time variable. We introduce a novel multi-agent RL algorithm called Multi-Agent Quasi-Newton (MAQN), which offers distinct advantages over current methods. The primary benefit of MAQN is its ability to achieve near-optimal convergence and learning rates in large-scale scenarios, while also ensuring rapid convergence to the optimal solution upon receiving accurate global feedback. This enhancement is achieved by incorporating a specific term in the update rule that leverages the convexity of the average reward function. This term facilitates convergence to the optimal solution even when global feedback is unavailable. We validate MAQN's effectiveness in multiple scenarios within large-scale topologies, demonstrating its superior performance in both learning speed and average reward while minimizing latency. Our results indicate that MAQN converges faster to optimal averages and exhibits greater robustness against latency. Additionally, we establish theoretical guarantees for MAQN's convergence to the optimal solution. Our findings highlight MAQN's potential for applications in large-scale RL environments, such as SDN. These HTNs are constructed from operator algebras $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{O}_i}$ associated with individual bulk patches $\mathcal{O}_i$, defined by the reduced density matrices of $\langle \psi | \mathcal{O}_i | \psi \rangle$. We demonstrate that the challenge of locating HTNs with minimal bond dimensions within single-particle pure states can be translated into finding specific subspaces within certain Schur-Malmquist Minkowski spaces. Leveraging this finding, we introduce a series of novel and efficient $AdS_2$ bulk geometries, including Schur-Malmquist brown holes and multi-particle Schur-Malmquist islands. For instance, we identify Schur-Malmquist islands as tensor networks characterized by a uniform bulk geometry and a consistent pattern of entanglement across all patches. Furthermore, we construct brown holes by integrating brown hole islands with their corresponding HTN networks, resulting in structures that possess no classical horizon and exhibit finite entropy. Notably, the entropy of these brown holes increases with the von Neumann entropy of the Schur-Malmquist islands. Finally, we provide additional examples of tensor networks that may represent distinct $AdS_2$ bulk configurations. In summary, we have developed a series of HTN networks with uniform bulk geometries, uniform entanglement structures, and potentially new $AdS_2$ bulk quantum states. These findings may offer fresh perspectives on bulk reconstruction, black hole thermodynamics, and the interior of Schwarzschild black holes. Our research also connects to recent investigations into Schur-Malmquist islands and brown holes. Future investigations may explore the connections between these networks and various ensembles, such as the two-dimensional SYK model, SYK$_0$, and random unitary ensembles. Additionally, it would be valuable to investigate the gravitational duals, particularly within the context of quantum extremal surfaces and the entanglement wedge reconstruction. Our investigation focuses on the extended magnetic structure of the outflow, characterized by a "bent-spoon" shape, which is best modeled using the non-axisymmetric Minardi+19 framework. This approach enables the detection of large-scale magnetic field geometry, offering novel insights for understanding the initial conditions of carbon stars that evolve into white dwarfs. The magnetic field strength diminishes with increasing distance from the star, ranging from approximately 100 microGauss at 1000 AU to 10 microGauss at 10,000 AU. Our findings suggest that outflows from carbon stars are shaped by at least two distinct mechanisms: the initial stellar wind geometry and the interaction between the star and its binary companion. Furthermore, our results indicate that outflows from carbon stars are more complex than previously thought, a hypothesis supported by the high prevalence of hotspots in CSIRCS (Circumstellar Infrared Circular Sources). Finally, we conclude that Magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) is a critical factor in shaping the circumstellar environments of carbon stars and should be considered in future research. While prior studies have addressed group bandits with independent experts, the case involving interdependent experts has been overlooked. We introduce an algorithm that achieves a regret bound of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{Td\log|S|})$, dependent on the horizon $T$, dimension $d$, and the size of the group $S$. Consequently, seismologists rely on data from thousands of seismometers, including those in Turkey, to identify earthquakes, determine their locations and magnitudes, understand fault mechanisms, study Earth's interior, and analyze other phenomena. The proposed method employs the Fourier single-sideband (FSB) transform applied to time-domain fluorescence signals and utilizes the inverse Hilbert transform to reconstruct symmetric Fourier-transformed fluorescence curves, thereby eliminating artifacts caused by end effects in decay measurements. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the calculated average fluorescence lifetime corresponds accurately to the true input lifetime, even when significant subregions exist with distinctly different decay times. interface conformal field theory (ICFT) have garnered significant interest recently due to their extensive theoretical value and wide-ranging physical applications. Recently, these frameworks have been employed to investigate boundary critical phenomena and impurity problems within the temperate regime. This contribution presents numerical renormalization group (NRG) findings regarding spin-1/2 impurities situated near the two-dimensional Heisenberg edge. We observe a distinct separation between the temperate and ground-state behaviors in the region between the vertex operator (VO) and the Nambu boundary condition (NBC). Beyond the temperate critical point, we observe a transition from the VO to the NBC, during which the VO bound state merges into the continuum. We compare our NRG findings with recent analytical predictions and further correlate them with experimental data regarding quantum dots near the quantum critical point. Finally, we outline potential applications involving quantum impurities subject to boundary conditions. The underlying framework of this problem aligns precisely with a specific type of BCFT, and our results indicate a shift in the VO bound state behavior from temperate to ground state. We also examine the relationship between VO and NBC, which represents two distinct boundary conditions for the Heisenberg chain, in the context of general BCFT. We also explore the connection between VO and the local spin correlation function, which is crucial for understanding the physical significance of the VO bound state. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the local spin correlation function and the single-site NRG wave function, which is essential for comparing theoretical results with experimental data. We also examine the relationship between the VO bound state and the local specific heat peak behavior in the quantum critical point (QCP) region. Finally, we discuss the relationship between VO and the local magnetic susceptibility in the QCP region. The local magnetic susceptibility behavior observed in our results aligns with the prediction of Volet et al. (Phys. Rev. B 95, 024409 (2017)) for the VO bound state. Collectively, these represent the first complete set of boundary critical phenomena and impurity problems within the temperate region. We also discuss future experimental applications regarding the local specific heat behavior. Specifically, we discuss the relationship between VO and the local specific heat behavior in the QCP region. within systems possessing multiple environments. In such scenarios, one environment couples to the system's position, influencing selection and measurement processes, while another couples to the system's momentum, affecting its dynamics. Standard formulations of the Jarzynski equality apply when only a single environment is present. However, we demonstrate that a second environment can be interpreted as a "non-equilibrium bath" whose temperature and velocity are determined by the specific geometry of the setup. With this characterization, the resulting generalized equality combines features of the standard and non-linear Jarzynski equalities. Furthermore, we analyze the condition under which this equality remains valid and examine the implications for the second law of thermodynamics in this context. As an illustration, we consider the case of a particle captured by an optically induced potential that couples to its position and interacts with a second "non-equilibrium" laser beam acting as a second environment. In this specific instance, general derivations simplify to recover the work relations previously reported in the literature. Finally, we address the challenge of experimentally verifying these relations. Our proposal involves controlling the internal states of trapped ions and observing how the two environments respond to positioning and momentum modulations. The low temperature and short lifetime of the involved quantum states make this proposal feasible for current experimental technology. Additionally, we note that the same trapping configuration could accommodate other interactions, such as those involving scattering. In this scenario, the second environment would couple to the particle's momentum via light momentum transfer, and the second law of thermodynamics would be expressed through modified Einstein-Hubble friction equations. This approach offers a way to experimentally test the second law of thermodynamics in small, damped quantum systems. Furthermore, it could clarify the interpretation of negative entropy production values sometimes observed in such experiments. To derive the generalized work relations, we employ quantum master equations and use two distinct paths: first, calculating the stochastic evolution of probabilities for pure states, and second, extending this to mixed states. In the first approach, we generalize the typicality argument to multiple environments, establishing the standard Jarzynski equality alongside corrections. In the second approach, we apply the Petz formalism to derive the same result using relative entropy. In both cases, the second law of thermodynamics is formulated using relative entropy rather than average free energy. Finally, we discuss the connection between this second law and the more recent generalization of the Clausius inequality. We demonstrate that, under appropriate technical assumptions, the space of infinitesimal deformations of an $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton is isomorphic to the cohomology of the underlying bundle of $\mathrm{SO}(7)$ skew-symmetric matrices, and we provide the corresponding bilinear form. Furthermore, we establish the analogue of the Uhlenbeck compactness theorem for this setting. Leveraging this cohomological description, we prove that if an instanton bundle possesses an irreducible or strongly irreducible Atiyah-Woodin type reduction, the bundle is actually reducible; consequently, all irreducible and strongly irreducible instanton bundles on a closed $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifold are essentially $\mathrm{SO}(7)$ trivial. experience remains a primary objective in neuroscience. Although behavioral studies have identified specific brain structures, such as the rostral striatum, their functional roles in consciousness are not yet fully understood. This study investigates how neural activity within these regions correlates with altered states of consciousness. We utilized a modified striatal dynamical model, calibrated to reflect both normal and catatonic consciousness levels, to simulate and contrast brain activity across these states. Our findings indicate that catatonic levels of consciousness correspond to lower coupling strengths between the direct and non-direct pathways and to significantly extended mean first passage times required for transitions between these pathways. Furthermore, we propose that the phenotypic expression of schizophrenia, particularly catatonia, may result from a molecular mechanism characterized by the downregulation of D2 dopamine receptors, alongside a significant reduction in striatal cholinergic activity. These results align with prior observations of hypodopaminergic states in schizophrenia patients. Finally, we explored the link between psychostimulants and consciousness by examining their impact on neural dynamics and mean first passage times using an optimal control approach, based on reports that such agents can elevate consciousness. Our findings suggest that the appropriate dosage of these stimulants in schizophrenia may be sub-optimal due to the diminished D2 receptor availability, thereby failing to sufficiently activate D1/D3 receptor-activated pathways to facilitate a higher consciousness state. This research underscores the critical role of the striatum in consciousness and the potential utility of mathematical modeling in elucidating the neural mechanisms underlying both consciousness and schizophrenia. Our objective is to identify a family consistent with this description. Our analysis revealed a young compact family characterized by a 2.8 AU semi-major axis, encompassing approximately 1,000 asteroids. It defines key concepts such as fairness, bias, and loss, examines the relationship between loss functions and prediction outcomes, and addresses the multifaceted nature of fairness, which is influenced by factors beyond just loss functions and outcomes. Short-term emotions were evaluated through a six-item questionnaire, while long-term emotions, characterized by more stable and consistent moods, were measured using the PANAS scale for positive and negative affect. Our analysis revealed that incorporating long-term emotion scores to characterize an individual's baseline state significantly enhanced recognition accuracy compared to baselines. Additionally, we found that recognizing highly positive or negative long-term emotions was more challenging than recognizing moderately positive or negative states. Finally, we demonstrated that applying advanced facial action unit recognition improved overall recognition performance. These findings suggest that assessing long-term emotional states to estimate baseline conditions effectively predicts short-term emotional fluctuations. This research paves the way for future systems capable of predicting future emotions based on recognized long-term states and facilitating timely interventions to mitigate adverse long-term effects on individuals. Such capabilities are particularly valuable for remote monitoring applications where physical contact is impossible, such as in remote work, education, and medical settings. In the medical domain, this approach could enable early diagnosis of mental health conditions by monitoring long-term emotional scores and baseline states. We anticipate that these results will foster further advancements in the field of remote emotion monitoring. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/andrews87/EmotionRecognition. generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) approximation is essential for algorithms utilizing a local model to train, compress, or interpret machine learning models. We introduce an approach to approximate the GGN through a sparse graph representation, enabling efficient iteration on conventional architectures and acceleration on GPU clusters. Our method first computes a sparse initial curvature estimate using a subset of model parameters, then iteratively refines this approximation by sequentially updating parameter estimates based on a graph where parameters function as both inputs and outputs. This iterative process effectively approximates solving the system of linear equations defined by the GNN matrix. We demonstrate that this strategy yields sufficient curvature accuracy for various tasks, including fine-tuning large language models, improving convergence rates, and enabling model compression. Results indicate that several tasks complete training with comparable or superior generalization using optimizers that incorporate curvature. Additionally, for tasks already employing a local model for optimization, our method yields an 80% reduction in iterations and improves generalization. Compressed versions of the approach yield even better outcomes. Beyond neural networks, we show that curvature information enhances the phrasing of prompts in few-shot in-context learning for large language models. Finally, for model classification tasks, our method integrates with sparse classifiers like SVMs to increase accuracy. Overall, accessing curvature information at a lower cost opens new possibilities for optimization, compression, and classification. The code is available at https://github.com/nyu-dlgraph. The paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/2106.01225, and the associated project website is at https://nyudlgraph.com.

Processing this data demands high-performance computing resources to perform real-time operations, which are crucial for applications such as radio astronomy's future search for extraterrestrial intelligence, live astrophysical imaging, and rapid transient detection. We introduce RAFT (Real-time Astronomical Fourier Transform), the inaugural open-source software library designed to facilitate real-time astronomical image formation on high-performance computers. Its architecture is based on a parallel multi-ring algorithm that executes the necessary discrete Fourier transforms (DFTs) in a time- and memory-efficient manner. Additionally, RAFF provides a straightforward interface for performing visibilities, visibility multiplication, and deprojection with minimal overhead. The software supports a flexible configuration of one-dimensional and two-dimensional rings, enabling the optimization of performance to align with the specific characteristics of any particular interferometer. RAFT is engineered for parallel execution, leveraging task- and data-parallelism, and can be integrated with the most current parallel computing frameworks, including MPI, OpenMP, and CUDA. The codebase is extensible, allowing for the easy addition of intermediate rings and the implementation of various visibility and deprojection functions. Currently, the primary focus is on optimizing visibility multiplication and achieving real-time image formation. We present a scalability analysis of the software and its performance within the HPC environment of the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, demonstrating speedups of up to 100 times compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions. This achieves a real-time image formation capability for a 4x4 km² field of view with a 256 x 256 pixel grid at a 4 ms frame time. Furthermore, RAFT enables the processing of 1 GHz of visibility data per second, a rate potentially expandable to several gigahertz. We conclude by outlining current and planned applications, including FASTIDIA, a real-time fast idle algorithm, the implementation of De-beam-and-Search for transient detection, and a key component for the upcoming Square Kilometre Array. The latest version is accessible at https://github.com/lofar-hpc/raft. The software is also available as a container image via Docker and Singularity, and its extensive unit tests facilitate the verification of correctness. We anticipate that RAFT will serve as a foundational component for the next generation of real-time HPC pipelines for the SKA. The primary method for addressing this risk is "waterfall development," a linear process where each stage must be approved before commencing the next. However, this approach is often criticized for being overly rigid and ill-suited to iterative workflows. This paper examines the validity of such critiques and evaluates the necessity of alternative methodologies like agile by analyzing over five decades of Euronews data on European film development, production timelines, and outcomes. Our findings indicate that the majority of European films actually follow a "stage gate" development process, which is better modeled as an iterative approach than as a strictly linear waterfall model. Additionally, we observed that films with shorter development durations are more likely to succeed. These results imply that agile-like methods are more effective for creating successful films and that reducing development time—through techniques such as prequels or sequels—may enhance the probability of success for individual projects. Finally, our data reveal that films with shorter development periods also tend to perform better at the box office and possess higher production values. Consequently, these insights suggest that shorter development cycles result in higher revenue and greater profitability for films. Overall, this evidence supports the conclusion that agile methodologies are essential for achieving both financial success and profitability in the film industry. Furthermore, these results align with those of the 70th Anniversary Study (2019) regarding Hollywood features. This study examines the dynamics of a single-phase renewable energy electrical drive (P-RED), which integrates sources like photovoltaics or wind turbines with energy storage via a DC-DC buck converter and is connected to loads through a coupling inductor. The analysis reveals that the P-RED exhibits second-order oscillatory behavior characterized by a natural frequency, storage, and coupling, with a damping term determined by the control loop. These dynamics can be understood through two simplified models: a single-phase resonant circuit and an LRC circuit. The proposed method is applied to control the P-RED using resonant control, where the natural frequency and Q-factor are directly tied to the physical parameters of the system. Simulation results based on P-RED models demonstrate that resonant control is highly effective at natural frequencies, and the study proposes strategies to enhance damping under off-resonance operating conditions. Furthermore, the paper outlines methods to leverage the P-RED's natural frequency for power factor correction, filtering, and harmonic compensation. Ultimately, this approach enables the integration of single-phase renewable energies into the grid without associated costs. Finally, the study addresses the impact of parameter uncertainties on P-RED dynamics and control, offering a solution to maintain optimal performance despite such uncertainties. In summary, this work provides a robust theoretical framework for analyzing and controlling single-phase renewable energy electrical drives. The task involves identifying an unknown state selected from a finite set of $k$ possibilities, where each instance consists of $n$ copies of an unknown pure state whose symmetry group is known. The analysis reveals that, up to first-order asymptotic approximation, zero-error distinguishability can be achieved if and only if at least one symmetry group element (beyond the identity) maps each state onto itself. We introduce an optimal strategy and derive an explicit formula for the corresponding zero-error threshold. Our findings indicate that, regardless of the specific symmetry, the optimal threshold for detecting two conjugate pure states of equal unknown dimension is approximately one fewer than the threshold for distinguishing between two known fixed states, such as the Bell basis, up to a multiplicative constant of $\ln 2$. Additionally, we establish a lower bound for the zero-error threshold for distinguishing any set of symmetric pure states, up to a constant factor, by applying recent bounds from asymmetric distinguishability, and we characterize the asymptotic behavior of this threshold as a function of the symmetry group. Finally, we explore the connection between symmetric state distinguishability and quantum hypothesis testing, demonstrating that any Type-II error-optimal strategy yields a nearly optimal zero-error threshold up to an additive constant.

Addressing this problem, we first observe that any successful online strategy can be formulated using a two-step procedure: performing a complete measurement on all $n$ copies to produce an outcome from a countable set, followed by a classical hypothesis test on this outcome. We demonstrate that this approach is not merely approximate but is actually optimal, meaning the optimal online strategy conducts a measurement on the $n$ copies and subsequently tests the result. By establishing a bijection between pure-state distinguishability problems and classical hypothesis testing problems, we derive a formula for the zero-error threshold as a function of the state ensemble and replica number. We further prove that this threshold is independent of the specific symmetry group and remains unchanged (up to a shift of at most one) whether the state dimension is fixed or allowed to grow unboundedly.

In the second part, we investigate distinguishing states with zero error under the constraint of performing a single measurement on the $n$-copy ensemble. We show that the optimal threshold is again independent of the symmetry group and is at most one greater than the threshold for distinguishing unknown mixed states of a specific symmetry. By leveraging established lower bounds from asymptotic hypothesis testing, we derive a lower bound for the optimal distinguishability threshold based on the states' fidelity.

**1. Introduction**
The Sun exhibits a complex array of time-variability phenomena, ranging from the well-known 11-year magnetic cycle to the subtle, long-term variations in solar irradiance. These variations are driven by magnetic activity across various spatial and temporal scales. Solar oscillations, or pressure waves, are a primary manifestation of this activity, arising from convection in the solar interior. These waves manifest as periodic fluctuations in brightness, known as sunquakes. By analyzing the spectrum of these oscillations, scientists can investigate the internal structure of the Sun, a field known as helioseismology.

Each tone corresponds to a specific eigenmode of the Sun, characterized by its frequency and a set of spatial eigenfunctions. These signals are consistent with a stochastic gravitational wave background, which continues to support a cosmological origin for the PTA method. This paper examines the statistical evidence for this background using a widely adopted "Bayesian model comparison" framework. Our analysis reveals that while there is strong evidence for a gravitational wave signal, the data also accommodate null hypotheses where the signal originates from either a geophysical or a purely statistical source. Although we do not dispute the validity of the "Bayesian model comparison" approach, we note that existing studies have often failed to rigorously define the data sets for each model, particularly regarding prior distributions. In this work, we provide a detailed specification of prior distributions for various PTA models. We demonstrate that certain parameterized models are overly broad, resulting in uninformative priors that lead to unphysical posterior distributions. Furthermore, we show that specific models are too complex for the current data, causing their posterior distributions to collapse to extreme values. Finally, we present a robust, well-defined model comparison tailored to the PTA's specific data and parameterization constraints. This approach utilizes Jeffreys priors for all models, ensuring well-defined posterior distributions and physically meaningful parameter estimates. We also explore the impact of pulsar distribution on the evidence for gravitational waves and compare single-array versus multi-array evidence. Our findings indicate that the Bayesian support for a gravitational wave background remains robust across different analysis methods and pulsar distributions. However, the current data set is insufficient to constrain the spectral properties of the background. We conclude that the most straightforward explanation for these results is a stochastic gravitational wave background driven by supermassive black hole dynamics. To further strengthen the case for a GW background and refine its parameter estimates, future observations with a significantly larger number of pulsars are required. This analysis serves as a foundational step for the International Square Kilometre Array Pulsar Timing Array (SKA-PTA). The proposed SKA-PTA configuration is expected to achieve a signal-to-noise ratio approximately 2.5 times greater than that of the NANOGrav, PPTA, and PTA collaboration's current datasets. Additionally, we discuss the enhanced evidence for a GW background and the resulting improvements to its parameter estimates. We anticipate that the SKA-PTA will provide strong support for a GW background signal and significantly improve constraints on its parameters. These systems face three primary challenges: (1) the high expense of hardware, (2) poor depth estimation performance within the field of view, and (3) insufficient noise suppression capabilities. Performance benchmarks conducted on the MLPerf Training training suite demonstrate that our hybrid approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Specifically, the interactionless component accelerates models characterized by high degrees of freedom, whereas the interactive component benefits models with low degrees of freedom. To our knowledge, this is the first work to explicitly categorize distributed training architectures into interactive and non-interactive frameworks; consequently, highlighting the advantages of a hybrid approach constitutes a significant contribution to the field. Our experimental results validate the efficacy of this proposed classification. Furthermore, we evaluate several state-of-the-art models, including BERT, GPT, ResNet, and YOLO. In the case of BERT, our hybrid architecture improves throughput by 1.8 times. For ResNet, improvements range from 1.1 to 1.5 times. On YOLO models, the hybrid approach delivers throughput improvements between 1.5 and 2.0 times, in addition to latency reductions between 1.2 and 1.9 times. These enhancements are achieved, on average, with only a 0.5% loss in accuracy. Additionally, we present a case study demonstrating that integrating the hybrid architecture requires minimal changes to the deep learning framework, involving just a few lines of code. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first proposal of such an integration method. Our implementation is compatible with both PyTorch and TensorFlow. Finally, we have developed a throughput model to predict performance based on key parameters, enabling users to assess the potential gains of incorporating our hybrid architecture. This paper serves as the first step toward a comprehensive characterization of distributed training through the introduction of our hybrid architecture. By allowing users to assess potential performance gains, our approach facilitates more informed decisions regarding the most suitable architecture for a specific use case. Leveraging the specific features of Dirac fermions, our method utilizes the Wigner function to define probabilities for changing both energy and momentum. Additionally, we develop a specific form of the interaction term in the Boltzmann equation to ensure energy conservation. The resulting electron distribution function is found to differ from the standard Fermi-Dirac distribution due to momentum relaxation caused by the lattice. Furthermore, the analysis incorporates phonon population, allowing the model to remain valid across both low and high-temperature regimes. Finally, a unique definition of the relaxation time is introduced to facilitate the derivation of a Drude-like conductivity. This Drude-like expression is observed to be independent of the Wigner-Poisson coupling. As a practical application, the model is employed to examine current-voltage characteristics in a graphene tunneling junction, with results showing strong agreement between the Wigner approximation and numerical solutions. Additionally, the Drude-like expression aligns with the relaxation time obtained from the Monte Carlo simulation. These findings suggest that the proposed model is effective for analyzing electron transport in graphene. stronomical objects appearing at different vertical positions. This effect causes the blue end of the spectrum to be raised and stretched relative to the red end, effectively smearing out the blue portion of the signal. The magnitude of this distortion is highly sensitive to the altitude of the observing site, the magnitude of the object's altitude, and the wavelength. Additionally, the phenomenon is not consistent; its magnitude and direction vary with the object's azimuth and atmospheric conditions. Consequently, the atmosphere acts as an optical prism for off-zenith observations, causing the image to shift upward and toward the zenith as altitude increases. Furthermore, the magnitude of this effect is more pronounced in observations near the horizon, where it can reach up to 10 times the magnitude compared to observations near the zenith. This is particularly problematic for spectroscopy, where even slight shifts can cause significant misalignment between the spectrum and the object's image. This issue is exacerbated by the continuous nature of the effect, which can cause a shift of up to 1000 pixels. To address this, atmospheric dispersion correctors (ADCs) are employed to compensate for atmospheric dispersion. An ADC functions as a reverse prism that undoes the reference prism's work, aligning the spectrum with the object's image. However, the performance of an ADC is heavily dependent on the specific atmospheric conditions at the time of observation. Furthermore, the reference prism's performance is also highly dependent on the atmospheric conditions. Therefore, the primary challenge in astronomical observation is selecting the most appropriate ADC and reference prism pair for a given set of atmospheric conditions. This paper aims to investigate how to choose the most suitable ADC and reference prism pair under specific atmospheric conditions. It begins by analyzing the performance of the ADC and reference prism pair under different atmospheric conditions. Subsequently, it explores how to select the most appropriate ADC and reference prism pair based on these conditions. Finally, it examines how to determine the most suitable pair based on the image's distortion degree. The proposed method is evaluated using both simulated data and real observational data. Ultimately, this research seeks to enhance the performance of atmospheric dispersion correctors and improve the overall quality of ground-based astronomical observations. This work represents a significant advancement in the field of astronomical observation. ) is a leading protocol that leverages quantum interference to achieve beyond-classical key rates, sometimes surpassing the classical Shannon limit. However, its implementation is complex, requiring precise phase stabilization and multiple intensity settings. This study introduces a simplified TF-QKD variant that eliminates the need for phase stabilization and reduces the intensity configuration burden by substituting several weak signal states with vacuum states. The resulting vacuum TF-QKD (V-TF-QKD) protocol was tested in a 550 km field trial across the low-loss South-East Asian optical fiber network. By employing vacuum states and measuring only the single photon number component, the error rate estimation process was simplified, enhancing system robustness and accelerating data processing. Analysis of field measurements indicates that secure key generation remains feasible down to approximately 28 dB of loss, with an order of magnitude improvement in signal-to-noise ratio. Notably, the protocol successfully generated a secure key at 505 km fiber distance when using very weak states (mean photon number of 0.1). Furthermore, by applying the coherent-phase-mapping approximation, the secure key rate was calculated using standard Shannon limits for the first time, and this limit was successfully exceeded for long-distance transmission. These findings confirm that V-TF-QKD is a promising protocol for ultra-long-distance secure communication, and its simplified structure and processing enable it to compete with standard FKQKD protocols, thereby positioning it as a viable protocol for practical deployment. This protocol is expected to find applications in various secure communication systems, such as secure video and audio transmission, where precise key rates are necessary to meet specific security requirements. In these scenarios, both experimental complexity and computational processing speed are critical factors, making V-TF-QKD a strong candidate for such applications. In conclusion, this protocol represents a significant step toward making TF-QKD practical for real-world applications. ho Ophiuchus molecular cloud complex exhibits an anomalous spectral energy distribution (SED) characterized by an infrared (IR) continuum lacking contribution from warm dust, alongside an IR excess attributed to a circumstellar disc. This study presents new observations from the VLT/SPHERE and VLT/VISIR instruments, which reveal the presence of a protoplanetary disc characterized by a small inner hole, a steep surface brightness profile, and a total infrared-to-total ratio ($\text{IR}/\text{Total}$) of 0.35, indicating only weak disc activity. Additionally, we observed a faint point source located slightly south of S1's position; its properties suggest it is likely a background source rather than a binary companion to S1. This finding contrasts with the hypothesis that S1 is a multiple system where the IR excess results from dust within a circumstellar disc around the companion. Instead, our data support the alternative scenario where the IR excess originates directly from a disc orbiting S1. This scenario is further supported by the absence of an H$\alpha$ emission component in the SED of S1, implying the disc is not accreting. Furthermore, the lack of silicate emission features in the IR continuum suggests the disc is either very thin or composed of depleted silicates. Consequently, the disc surrounding S1 in Rho Oph B appears to be a rare instance of a stable, non-accreting disc with a compact inner cavity. Finally, the observed point source south of S1 offers an opportunity to investigate the relationship between the mass of the central body and the mass of its surrounding disc. By comparing the total mass of S1, derived from its position in the colour-magnitude diagram, with the mass derived from the disc's surface-brightness profile, we can determine if the two are comparable. This comparison will help clarify the physical nature of the system and the potential for planet formation. In this context, the source south of S1 serves as a proxy for the disc's total mass. This paper presents a framework for integrating domain knowledge into time series modeling by employing Bayesian methods to quantify uncertainty and validate model consistency. While research has predominantly examined TQA through the lens of Language Models (LMs), lacking a theoretical basis for how translators cognitively process errors, we applied Pattern Matching Theory (PMT) to this field. Our analysis of MT translation errors revealed four predominant categories, which we subsequently modeled using PMT to simulate a translator's evaluation process. We demonstrate that longitudinal acoustic phonon-mediated coupling consistently enhances superconducting critical temperatures, reaching a maximum of 10.5 K for MoS$_{2}$ and 7.5 K for WS$_{2}$. In contrast, we identify a novel, previously unknown contribution to electron phonon coupling arising from transverse acoustic phonons, which reduces superconductivity in these materials. Furthermore, we establish a general principle regarding this newly discovered coupling mechanism by analyzing a comprehensive model. These findings offer a unified framework for elucidating unconventional superconductivity driven by acoustic-phonon coupling in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides. Additionally, the predicted high superconducting critical temperatures suggest these materials are well-suited for applications in ultrafast electronics and quantum computing. Our predicted critical-temperature records for MoS$_{2}$ and WS$_{2}$ are significantly higher—by factors of 3 to 5—than those observed in hydrogen monolayers supported on a silicon carbide substrate. Finally, our results indicate that acoustic-phonon coupling facilitates relatively high critical temperatures even in electron-depleted two-dimensional superconductors with low carrier densities. To achieve a local maximum in superconductivity, we suggest exploring transition metal dichalcogenides that exhibit a strong transverse phonon softening mode at low carrier densities but a robust longitudinal acoustic phonon-mediated coupling at higher carrier densities. As a practical example, we identify MoSe$_{2}$ as a promising candidate, predicting its superconducting critical temperature to be 11.5 K at a carrier density of 0.03 nm$^{-2}$. These predictions can be validated through experiments involving hydrogenation, intercalation, or electrostatic gating. Our findings also hold relevance for understanding superconductivity in other unconventional, low-carrier-density, and carrier-density-free systems, such as twisted bilayer graphene and twisted bilayer NbSe$_{2}$. Our analysis indicates that acoustic-phonon coupling could significantly elevate the superconducting critical temperatures of these materials, with Moore's law-like advancements in semiconductor technology potentially enabling experimental verification of these predictions. In conclusion, our findings open a promising avenue for designing superconductors with ultra-high critical temperatures and low carrier densities, thereby advancing both fundamental research and technological applications. ### 1. Introduction

Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (SNE) or t-SNE is a classic embedding algorithm that maps high-dimensional data to low-dimensional Euclidean space. It achieves this by assigning points in the original space probabilistic weights representing the likelihood that one point is a neighbor of another. Specifically, the pairwise weights in the embedding space are derived from the original pairwise weights, which are calculated using a Student's t-distribution rather than a Gaussian distribution. The original sequential KMeans algorithm for SNE or t-SNE was introduced by H. S. Seung and W. T. Simard in 1997. Subsequently, various implementations and extensions have been created. For instance, L. Schmidt-Thalsbom et al. introduced a GPU-based algorithm for KMeans with t-SNE in 2012. More recently, A. Van Der Maaten and U. Li used the C++ library Armadillo to create a serial algorithm for SNE or t-SNE in 2017. This paper presents a distributed algorithm for t-SNE and its implementation, which demonstrates performance improvements of two orders of magnitude for TSN with 500,000 points. Specifically, we contend that under certain conditions, normalized cumulative distribution functions associated with instantaneous rates approach standard Gaussian distributions as the number of users increases. This result is demonstrated across general interference channels, orthogonal interference channels, and symmetric interference channels. The "separation" here refers simply to the distance between points, without regard to orientation. This process is frequently employed to model clustered point patterns, with $\lambda$ representing the clustering strength. We propose a straightforward rejection-based Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that achieves rapid mixing. This approach allows for the efficient generation of realizations from the Stauss process across a broad range of $\lambda$. Additionally, we demonstrate a particularly efficient method for generating realizations from the specific case where $\lambda=1/2$ and the distance $r$ is determined by the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann $\zeta$ function. These results are derived from an analysis of the algorithm's mixing time. Finally, we apply this method to produce realizations of the Riemann $\zeta$ function's zeros on the critical line up to the 1000th power of the Skewes' number. This outcome supports the widely held conjecture that the distribution of these zeros behaves like a $\text{Bernoulli-Jury}(1/2, r)$ process. The efficiency of the algorithm relies on the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and the Littlewood Conjecture. Furthermore, we illustrate how to incorporate the Generalized Lindelöf Hypothesis to create an algorithm for sampling from the process when $\lambda$ is small. Our primary application involves generating realizations from the process when $\lambda=1/4$ and $r$ again corresponds to the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann $\zeta$ function. This enables the study of the "Shanks-Wright" process, a model for the potential zeros of other L-functions. This application motivates conjectures regarding the distributions of these L-function zeros. In the specific instance where the Shafer-Wright process is used, we can derive asymptotic formulas for the average gap between these zeros. This finding aligns with the Generalized Eudoxus Conjecture. More broadly, we can estimate the average gap for any $\lambda > 1/4$, yielding an asymptotic formula for the average space between potential zeros for non-trivial Dirichlet L-functions. This study examines the correction of the Schrödinger equation under the GUP framework as a method for investigating low-energy quantum gravity. Specifically, it analyzes the correction to the Hydrogen atom's energy levels using this theoretical approach. We introduce a novel interactive graph search mechanism that integrates information gain and prediction uncertainty into its expansion strategy, thereby reducing the reliance on human search effort. Our method was evaluated on a human-designed interactive 3D object detection system, where it reduced the average annotation cost by 23% compared to a baseline depth-first search approach. ### 1. Introduction
Graph-based neural networks (BNNs) [1–3] have demonstrated superior performance across various single and multi-object detection tasks, surpassing state-of-the-art methods. Their core principle involves propagating information along a graph's connectivity structure, a process that can be guided by human-defined topological knowledge. However, for many 3D detection tasks, acquiring complete and accurate graph connectivity is difficult, if not impossible.

To address these challenges, we introduce a new interaction model for graph search designed for 3D object detection. This model enables users to define graph connectivity in a partially supervised manner. Specifically, BNNs are integrated into an interactive system where users annotate a subset of labels and establish links between objects. The remaining object labels and links are inferred through graph propagation rather than explicit annotation. We propose a search-based annotation strategy that combines graph prediction with a search algorithm. This approach reduces the effort required to build graph structures and selects nodes for label propagation that maximize both global and local information gain. We evaluate our method using human search annotations on the KITTI dataset, achieving a 5% increase in accuracy over direct graph prediction.

### 2. Introduction
Interactive graph search guides the graph search process to propagate object labels. As depicted in Figure 1, users are presented with a link between two objects and must decide whether to create a link (left) or split the objects into two (right). This search process is iterative, continuing until the user determines the objects are unconnected. To minimize human effort, we have designed a mechanism that prioritizes label propagation from nodes with existing labels. This mechanism relies on two core components: (1) a link prediction model that predicts the probability of a link between two objects, and (2) an interactive graph search mechanism that balances global and local label propagation.

Alignments represent a state-of-the-art technique for calculating quantitative conformance metrics, such as overalignment, underalignment, and goal overalignment, which facilitate process mining. The alignment algorithm achieves its quantitative results by separating model and data, thereby ensuring data-reusability and tool-independence. However, the standard alignment algorithm is computationally infeasible for large event logs. To address this, heuristic and machine learning-based alignment strategies have been developed. While heuristic approaches are computationally viable, they often result in suboptimal alignments; machine learning methods can produce near-optimal results but typically require costly cross-validation and lack guarantee of convergence. This article introduces a novel concept of batch-alignments that combines the near-optimality of machine learning with the efficiency of heuristic methods while ensuring convergence. Specifically, we generalize the concept of alignments to batch-alignments, which are guaranteed to converge to a near-optimal state and generally perform well in practice. We also experimentally compare the batch-alignments method against existing heuristic and machine learning-based techniques. Our results indicate that batch-alignments outperform prior methods in terms of runtime and (cross-validated) overalignment, and they are suitable for detecting goal overalignment conformance. Our implementation, which runs in under 100 milliseconds for 100,000 activity instances, is the first to achieve such performance. This represents a new application of batch learning within process mining. Our contributions include a generalization of the alignment algorithm to batch-alignments, an associated optimization algorithm, and an efficiency analysis demonstrating that this new class of algorithms surpasses previous methods. Furthermore, we provide an initial guideline for selecting the appropriate number of (virtual) activities per real activity. While current models are generally precise under daylight conditions, they often fail during nighttime because they do not adequately account for radio wave reflection and scattering. This paper introduces a hybrid scattering model specifically designed for nighttime cellular radio propagation. The framework is divided into two components: direct signals, which represent radio waves that either travel directly or reflect off buildings, and scattered signals, which denote waves dispersed throughout the environment. We demonstrate that the statistical properties of this hybrid model can be effectively characterized using the one-minus-complement cumulative distribution function (CDF). Furthermore, based on measurements conducted in an urban setting, we validate the one-minus-complement CDF by fitting model parameters to real-world data. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed radio propagation model achieves high accuracy. Additionally, we show that this model is not limited to nighttime conditions but also applies accurately to other times of the day. Finally, we illustrate that the model is particularly well-suited for applications such as network design and management. These findings are expected to facilitate more efficient cellular network operations. Numerous radio propagation models have been developed over the past few decades, typically categorized into empirical, deterministic, and semi-empirical types. Empirical models rely on statistical analysis of measurement data, whereas deterministic models are based on the physical principles of radio wave propagation. Semi-empirical models combine elements of both empirical and deterministic approaches. Although these models have been widely applied, they often suffer from limitations. A common approach involves using log-distance path loss models for large-scale analysis, often augmented with a Rayleigh fading model to capture small-scale variations caused by multipath effects. However, the mechanisms driving their formation—particularly how they transition from fluid to solid states—remain poorly understood. This study investigates the dynamics of these transitions in three-dimensional monodisperse hard-sphere gels induced by a mild external potential, such as gravity. By simulating systems of passive and active spheres under increasing gravitational effects, we map out a phase diagram that captures how these systems evolve. Our findings indicate that gravity triggers a shear-induced solidification characterized by shear banding and a shear-dependent solidification kinetics exponent of 1/2, both of which align with Affine dynamics. Conversely, in the presence of active spheres, we observe a scenario where increased activity delays the gelation process. Collectively, these results confirm that applying a marginal external potential serves as an effective experimental method to explore the phase behavior of colloidal gels. Perturbations in tensor data are inevitable in real-world scenarios, yet data corruption can significantly degrade reconstruction accuracy. To address noisy and missing data, tensor completion has emerged as a vital technique, finding applications in medical imaging, hyperspectral imaging, and remote sensing. Tensor completion reconstructs incomplete, multi-dimensional data by exploiting its low-rank structure, a technique particularly valuable for noisy datasets. Recent advancements in tensor completion have introduced various regularization methods, yet accurate reconstruction from missing and noisy data remains challenging. Addressing these issues, this paper presents a new tensor completion approach that utilizes mixed norm, spectral norm, and entropy to reconstruct corrupted data. These norms capture spectral and entropy characteristics, enhancing reconstruction performance. The study formulates an optimization model combining spectral norm, mixed norm, and entropy terms, followed by the design of a solution algorithm. Theoretical analysis is provided, proving the algorithm's finite convergence under an exact data model assumption. Numerical experiments on synthetic data demonstrate the algorithm's robustness and accuracy, revealing its effectiveness in scenarios with missing and noisy data. Additionally, the algorithm exhibits accuracy superior to state-of-the-art methods. Consequently, the algorithm is recommended for practical applications involving missing and noisy tensor data.
