Although prior research has addressed learning these non-intentional actions, it often fails to simultaneously identify both short-term intentions (such as sub-task goals) and long-term intentions (such as the overall task objective). To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework that learns compact representations of these actions to determine long-term goals, while employing a reinforcement learning strategy to capture short-term intentions. This framework is utilized to learn a human operator's behavior when navigating a navigation task within a robot-assisted surgical environment. The proposed approach successfully infers long-term goals from actions that differ significantly from the intended program, whereas intentionality fields derived from these local, short-term goals enable the robot to adapt its execution to the operator's specific actions. Experimental results confirm that the proposed method effectively generalizes to novel tasks and to robotic operators with distinct behavioral characteristics. Furthermore, a human factors study demonstrates that the long-term goals inferred by the system align with those intended by the human participants. These findings indicate that the system can reliably detect long-term intentions, thereby enhancing transparency and fostering trust between the robot and the operator. The source code is available at https://github.com/robo-surgery. We demonstrate that Long-term Goal Inference can serve as a critical module for robotics, enabling autonomous goal adaptation and flexible re-planning in dynamic environments. This allows robots to better support human operators in complex scenarios. Additionally, we show that Long-term Goal Inference can function as a key component for autonomous goal adaptation and re-planning in dynamic settings, significantly reducing the programming effort required to deploy such robots in diverse real-world situations. The long-term objective is to integrate this system with other large-scale goal adaptation and re-planning mechanisms. This combination would enable robotic systems to dynamically adjust to human operators in complex settings, substantially reducing the amount of programming needed. Finally, we illustrate that this approach can facilitate autonomous goal adaptation and re-planning, helping robots better assist human users in complex settings. By reducing the need for manual programming, the system enhances usability and efficiency. The primary issue remains that most path planning methods are highly dependent on the specific application and the available a-priori information. This paper introduces a novel approach called the Contextual Planning Graph (CPG), which incorporates real-time environmental features and the robot's current trajectory to determine the optimal next action. By integrating contextual awareness into trajectory optimization, the method reduces reliance on pre-existing path data and enables the continuous planning of globally optimal paths. The study also examines how including or excluding certain environmental features affects the CPG and the resulting paths. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that utilizing continuous context information allows for a more compact and simplified representation of the CPG. Experimental results in a real-world office setting show that the CPG reduces the average number of steps a mobile robot needs to take to reach a target by 20% compared to other path planning techniques. Additionally, the proposed approach decreases the computational cost of high-frequency path planning on graphs by at least 50% while maintaining global optimality. Leveraging contextual information also enhances the robustness of the generated paths against dynamic obstacles. Finally, the authors show that integrating the CPG with a lightweight deep reinforcement learning agent creates a highly efficient hybrid system for real-time navigation. The research concludes with an analysis of the robot's behavior and the characteristics of the planned paths. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ahmadyar/Contextual-Planning-Graph. the demand for high-speed data transmission, making millimeter-wave (mmWave) radio a critical solution for next-generation applications. This progress has been driven primarily by the widespread availability of low-cost semiconductor materials. However, mmWave signals are inherently susceptible to attenuation caused by absorption in air and solid objects. Although recent research indicates that human body movements can scatter these signals effectively enough to enable line-of-sight (LoS) communication, the impact of static environments on mmWave signal propagation remains underexplored. This study investigates the statistical characteristics of mmWave propagation within typical indoor offices. Using measurements from an 8×8 mmWave antenna array operating at 28 GHz, we analyzed the signal propagation behavior in environments without moving objects. Our findings indicate that while mmWave signals can penetrate walls, they undergo substantial attenuation, often resulting in a strong obstructed path that exceeds the power of the direct non-line-of-sight (NLoS) path. We demonstrate that accurately estimating wall thickness and dielectric constants can effectively predict path power losses and facilitate millimeter-wave device discovery. These results highlight the significant impact of wall obstruction on mmWave signal propagation in static indoor offices, emphasizing the need to account for wall penetration effects in system design. Furthermore, we show that characterizing the physical properties of walls can be achieved through an integrated approach utilizing channel measurements and dielectric properties. Finally, we propose a method to enhance mmWave link robustness in static offices by implementing a wall discovery mechanism that leverages these physical characteristics. This approach demonstrates substantial performance gains compared to a baseline system without wall discovery. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of mmWave propagation in static indoor offices, aiding more effective millimeter-wave device discovery. X-ray astronomy datasets are typically derived from multiple instruments utilizing distinct X-ray sources; consequently, reconstructing a single object requires combining information across different CT slices. However, discrepancies between datasets from various instruments can hinder the accuracy of the reconstruction. To address this, we propose a two-step algorithm utilizing Total Variation (TV) regularization. First, a multi-slice deconvolution method based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) is developed to decouple and disentangle CT slices using the Mixed entropy metric. Following deconvolution, the algorithm reconstructs the object from all available information by solving a least squares problem with a quadratic data fidelity term, solved again via the ADMM method. Finally, TV regularization is applied to reduce noise and enhance the sharpness of the reconstructed edges. Our proposed method is evaluated on both simulated and experimental data, demonstrating that it successfully decouples and reconstructs the object while effectively preserving the distinct features and edges characteristic of each instrument. The complete open-source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ahmed-ibrahim12/DisentanglingCT. In this work, the term "CT" serves a general purpose. Specifically, we refer to the proposed algorithm for CT-like data, acknowledging that it can also be applied to other imaging modalities such as tomography or deconvolution. Furthermore, while ADMM is a widely used optimization technique, its application here is novel; therefore, we believe it is appropriate to refer to this approach as a new algorithm for CT-like data. Additionally, the paper presents a new entropy metric for decoupling and disentanglement, alongside a numerical comparison against other metrics. Finally, a novel method for calculating gradients and a metric for assessing reconstruction quality are introduced. This study is part of a broader effort to develop new algorithms for disentangling and decoupling CT-like data in astronomy and medicine, with a specific focus on X-ray imaging. The motivation for this research stems from the X-ray astronomy community, where combining information from datasets of similar wavelength ranges is crucial for achieving high-quality reconstructions. -ray pulse from a Free-Electron Laser (FEL) can induce rapid electronic changes within a material. These electronic shifts trigger subsequent nuclear motion, leading to structural transformations that occur on timescales ranging from femtoseconds to nanoseconds. We present a computer simulation framework designed to investigate both electronic and structural dynamics in materials, alongside the physical processes that generate absorption fluctuations in a thin-film gold sample. The simulation, built on the "shake, melt, and cool" model, integrates electronic relaxation, light-induced heating, and lattice dynamics. By simulating X-ray transmission through a stochastic ensemble of 10^8 nanoparticles, we analyze the mechanisms driving experimental absorption fluctuations. Our findings demonstrate that the absorbed energy, lattice temperature, and characteristic time scales for these fluctuations vary significantly across different materials. Specifically, for gold, the absorption and energy absorption rates exhibit a strong dependence on electron density, which is a direct consequence of electronic relaxation. Additionally, the absorption rate is highly sensitive to both the pump pulse duration and the detector's integration time. Finally, the absorption signal is shown to be affected by the sample's thickness. These results offer a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms responsible for ultrafast optical absorption changes in metals. The developed framework can be directly applied to study other elemental metals and alloys, as well as dielectrics and semiconductors. Furthermore, this study facilitates the design of experiments utilizing advanced X-ray sources like FELs. To address this, researchers have explored transfer learning techniques, including adapting pre-trained models to new tasks or languages. This paper introduces a novel method for training robust ASR models by leveraging information from multiple languages belonging to the same family. The approach combines Gaussian processes for physical parameters with Gaussian Markov decision processes to define the system's physical behavior. Unlike traditional data-driven deep learning methods, which can suffer from poor generalization when predicting dynamics outside the range of observed data, our approach leverages prior physical knowledge to achieve accurate predictions based on minimal data. Validated through simulations involving oscillating springs and an inverted pendulum on a cart, as well as real-world data from a robotic arm, we demonstrate that the proposed method enables precise parameter estimation and dynamic prediction using very small datasets. We present a framework for learning nonlinear dynamical systems by integrating Gaussian process models with Koopman operator theory. This approach yields a global, linear representation of nonlinear dynamics while offering uncertainty quantification and effective regularization for sparse, noisy data. The resulting model can be applied to various tasks, including system identification, prediction, control, and anomaly detection. To our knowledge, this is the first instance of uncertainty quantification in a nonlinear system via the Koopman perspective, achieved through a Bayesian learning framework. We evaluate the method on both simulated and real-world datasets, finding that it produces accurate predictions even for dynamics substantially different from those seen during training. This suggests that the approach can learn transferable features applicable to a wide range of systems. (More)

We introduce a novel method for learning a global linear model of nonlinear dynamics by unifying Gaussian processes with Koopman operator theory. By parameterizing the Koopman map using Gaussian processes, we establish a connection to sparse regression, allowing for efficient computation and uncertainty quantification. data from the ALMA Large Program "GALACTIC PLAnetary Survey for ALMA" (GALPALS), which targets the Galactic plane, has been conducted. This analysis focuses on a selected sample of 1,000 planetary systems, chosen from a larger catalog of nearly 2,000 systems derived from the NASA Exoplanet Archive (NEA). The systems are categorized into two groups based on NEA classification: one comprising planets orbiting within 1 au of their host stars, and the other including those orbiting beyond 1 au. Both samples exclude brown dwarfs and planets with masses less than 10 M_Earth. The study reports the spatial distribution of these systems and their associated dust mass in the circumstellar region. Additionally, a correlation is observed between dust mass and the stellar class of the host. This work is the first to examine the spatial distribution of planets as substructures of exoplanetary systems at a resolution of 0.034 au (equivalent to 1" at 1 pc). Furthermore, it is the first analysis to specifically investigate whether brown dwarfs and low-mass planets are distributed differently compared to other planets. The observed distribution indicates that planets are more abundant around low-mass stars, with no significant difference found between those inside and outside 1 au. However, brown dwarfs appear more concentrated around low-mass stars than low-mass planets do. Finally, the concentration of low-mass planets suggests that the most massive planets may reside within 1 au of their host stars. These findings align with the core accretion model of planet formation, which posits that giant planets form via the accumulation of solid particles via collision and coalescence. This hypothesis predicts a higher frequency of giant planets around low-mass stars, consistent with the higher dust mass detected around low-mass stars in our observations. Since the concentration of low-mass planets supports the core accretion model, the observed concentration of brown dwarfs also supports the theory that giant planets form through gravitational instability. These initial results from GALPALS will be expanded by the full dataset, which is expected to be published in a future publication. Furthermore, ALMA's sensitivity will enable the investigation of dust emission from planets at even smaller separations from their host stars. To address this, a future publication will explore how the disk mass required to form planets varies with distance from the star. This will be achieved by examining disk mass distribution relative to both stellar mass and planetary orbital distance

This study examines PBHs within the framework of noncommutative geometry (NG), where spatial coordinates exhibit a non-trivial commutation relation. Our findings indicate that PBHs in NG space possess lower masses compared to their counterparts in general relativity (GR). Consequently, the assumption that PBHs account for dark matter necessitates a specific NG-dependent mass threshold. We demonstrate that NG spacetime imposes an NG-dependent mass limit for PBHs. This paper introduces a novel approach that integrates cooperative optimization with system-level optimizations, such as quantization and sparsity, to achieve system-friendly parameter-efficient tuning. Our core concept involves partitioning the trainable parameters of a deep neural network into disjoint sub-networks, training each independently, and subsequently fine-tuning the collective network. Perturbations of this nature are essential for explaining both the dark matter observed today and the abundance of very high-energy cosmic rays. In this study, we propose a framework where such phase transitions produce hidden QCD axions through the "axion freeze-in" mechanism. The infrared scale of these transition events is hypothesized to align with the ultraviolet (UV) cutoff of a highly warped geometry, which simultaneously sets the energy scale for the DBI effect. We demonstrate that axion freeze-in can account for the observed extremely high-energy cosmic rays while remaining compatible with big bang nucleosynthesis. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the observed dark matter density and these cosmic rays, offering a novel explanation for their origin while maintaining consistency with established astrophysical constraints. Finally, we illustrate how this mechanism can determine the mass of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays. Our analysis indicates that hidden QCD axions with masses ranging from $10^{-12}$ eV to 10 eV are viable candidates for explaining these high-energy events. We anticipate that our proposed explanation will stimulate further research into the nature of these cosmic rays. Additionally, we show that this explanation remains consistent with recent observations from the IceCube collaboration. We conclude by examining the parameter space of various inflationary models capable of generating such axions and identifying a preferred model space. Our findings suggest that for a given axion mass, there exists a preferred scale for the UV cutoff of the warped geometry. This scale is notably small, approximately $10^{13}$ GeV, and is significantly lower than the high energy scales typically anticipated for string theory. The characteristic energy of these rays exhibits a step-like structure near $10^{20}$ eV, which can be interpreted as a consequence of axion freeze-in. Current methods often rely on back-projection of network activations to identify relevant inputs, but this requires gradient computation, which is infeasible for vision transformers and slow for convolutions. Furthermore, back-projecting activations fails to account for spatial relationships between inputs, a factor vital for place recognition and segmentation. a pivotal step toward understanding the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity. This study employs the high-temperature $\beta$-expansion method to analyze $\langle \rho^2 \rangle$, the squared thermal expansion coefficient, in a spin model incorporating both nearest-neighbor and second-neighbor Coulomb interactions. The $\beta$-expansion technique enables the systematic calculation of thermal properties for high-temperature equilibrium states. Our theoretical findings for $\langle \rho^2 \rangle$ align well with existing experimental data, collectively offering compelling evidence that the exchange of longitudinal spin fluctuations mediated by Coulomb interactions among holes is a primary cause of the unusually strong lattice coupling observed in cuprates. Consequently, these results support the hypothesis that local antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations are integral to the high-temperature superconducting mechanism. Finally, our findings are contrasted with recent proposals suggesting that electronic correlations are weak, despite the necessity of electron-electon interaction. In summary, this work underscores that Coulomb interactions between electrons and holes generate large exchange interactions and local antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations in cuprates. These features are fundamental to explaining the anomalously high phonon coupling observed in these materials. We propose that these characteristics can be effectively described by an effective phonon Hamiltonian involving antiferromagnetic nearest-neighbor and second-neighbor electron-phonon interactions. We anticipate that the resulting effective phonon Hamiltonian will facilitate the understanding of high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates. This phase is characterized by a large Fermi surface featuring significant nesting vectors, suggesting a strong candidate for antiferromagnetic long-range ordering. Our study details the structural and electronic properties of this phase using density functional theory (DFT) and compares them with our earlier high-pressure X-ray diffraction experiments on Mn. Our calculations predict a magnetic moment of $3.5\,\mu_B$ per atom, in close agreement with our experimental value of $3.4\,\mu_B$. However, both theoretical and electronic structure analyses indicate that the magnetic moments are not uniform; they vary spatially, being greater near the corner atoms and smaller near the body-center and edge-neighbor atoms. This non-uniformity is also supported by our experimental data. Additionally, we observe that the Fermi surface remains largely unchanged across different levels of exchange-correlation corrections, though it transforms from a three-dimensional to a two-dimensional structure when applying these variations. We further demonstrate that the electronic structure of Mn can be accurately described by incorporating magnetic moments that reflect these non-uniformities. While most existing research relies on single-modality inputs, integrating multi-modal data has been established as highly effective for various brain imaging tasks, yet its potential in recent deep learning frameworks remains unexplored. This study presents the first application of a joint learning strategy within a deep learning framework to facilitate the reconstruction of Rician noise-corrupted low-resolution brain images. Specifically, we developed the Joint learning model for Rician images and their Isotropic equivalents (JRIIE), which employs Rician and Isotropic inputs with identical dimensions to achieve the same (or equivalent) resolution. Our method leverages the complementary information across different noise distributions and across inputs from different imaging resolutions. Furthermore, the deep learning structure utilizes two ResNet blocks designed for capturing short-range and long-range correlations. Comprehensive experiments across multiple scenarios demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently surpasses traditional interpolation-based methods and state-of-the-art deep learning models. Additionally, the JRIIE delivers superior performance compared to its variant without joint learning on the real low-resolution MRI dataset. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed framework can be effectively extended to simulate super-resolution tasks. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhaoqianliu/RB_IM. This study examines helioseismic data regarding turbulence anisotropy, specifically the vertical versus horizontal components of velocity perturbations, to address the question of effective turbulence anisotropy. Our analysis focuses on the near-surface region of the photosphere, where turbulent energy dissipation is believed to occur. Our findings indicate that, within the most active turbulence zone, vertical turbulence is significantly stronger than horizontal turbulence, with a magnitude at least 50% greater. a market index. This process involves calculating the tracking difference, which measures the portfolio's under- or over-performance relative to the benchmark. While tracking difference is widely recognized, it is theoretically flawed because it conflates two distinct concepts: the relative return of the benchmark and the portfolio's idiosyncratic alpha. If left unaddressed, this confusion can lead managers to pursue inappropriate objectives, such as underinvesting in sectors that outperform but exhibit high volatility. Furthermore, relying solely on the tracking difference may cause managers to over-optimize, systematically tilting the portfolio away from the benchmark in pursuit of these spurious metrics.

This paper addresses these issues by first decomposing the tracking difference into market-related and idiosyncratic components to clarify its structure. Second, it introduces an objective function for portfolio managers that is independent of the benchmark, ensuring the tracking difference does not interfere with optimization. Third, it proposes a straightforward optimization procedure enabling the manager to directly control the tracking difference, thereby eliminating the benchmark's direct influence on the portfolio. Finally, backtesting across various portfolios demonstrates that an unoptimized portfolio fails to meet the manager's objectives, whereas the optimized versions successfully achieve them. All code utilized to generate these findings is publicly available. The results of this backtesting are expected to assist unoptimized managers in achieving their stated goals. Finally, this article serves as a platform for dialogue among practitioners regarding their portfolio optimization objectives. Future extensions could involve practitioners discussing their goals and adapting code to quantify these objectives.

This study investigates the chemical evolution of the massive dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, which has a stellar mass of $\log(M_*/M_{\odot}) = 8.8$ and a lookback time of approximately 9 Gyr. Utilizing integral field spectroscopy from the Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE), we analyzed the sample's chemical composition and kinematic data. The results reveal a metal-rich population with $[\rm{Fe/H}] \sim 0$ and $[\rm{O/H}] \sim 0$, distinguishing it from other dwarflies with stellar masses in the same range, such as NGC 5477 and NGC 5775, which exhibit lower metallicities ($[\rm{Fe/H}] \sim -0.5$ to $-1$). The NGC 5253 galaxy displays a homogeneous population with no significant spatial metallicity gradients, though it contains a small, highly metal-rich globular cluster population. Our findings indicate that NGC 5253 has undergone efficient chemical enrichment, likely driven by early, intense star formation. Additionally, the galaxy shows a distinct kinematic population characterized by higher velocities and elongated orbits, interpreted as an accreted dwarf galaxy that contributed to the growth of NGC 5253. This study demonstrates that even relatively simple dwarf galaxies can possess complex and heterogeneous populations, suggesting that similar complexity may exist in other transients and transients. Furthermore, the presence of a high-velocity population in NGC 5253 highlights the need for more detailed kinematic studies of other dwarf galaxies. Finally, we show that the globular cluster population in NGC 5253 is more metal-rich than the stellar population, implying that its clusters formed in a metal-poor environment. We conclude that NGC 5253 is a unique object that has contributed significantly to our understanding of galactic evolution. In this work, we establish a connection between generalizations of Bass's conjecture and categories of finitely generated modules over specific classes of Gorenstein rings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a newly defined functor concerning minimal injective resolutions induces a derived equivalence between modules over certain Artin algebras and those in certain categories of Gorenstein modules over Artin Gorenstein rings. Additionally, we provide an application of this functor to an old problem: we construct a functor from the module category of an Artin Gorenstein ring to the minimal injective injective core of its minimal injective resolution, proving that this functor is both full and faithful. Consequently, we derive an inequality comparing the global dimensions of these two categories. Since the minimal injective core of a minimal injective resolution is equivalent to the Gorenstein projective dimension, our findings imply an upper bound on the Gorenstein projective dimension of modules over Artin Gorenstein rings. Finally, for finite group algebras, we establish bounds on the Gorenstein projective dimension of Gorenstein modules, a class of modules that forms an abelian category. These results are extended to certain categories of Gorenstein modules. Our findings also contribute to a broader question: we generalize the boundedness of the Gorenstein projective dimension for finitely generated modules over Noetherian rings to boundedness within specific categories of Gorenstein modules over Gorenstein rings. This enables an extension of several recent findings, such as those in \cite{MinhThuy2021}, to these categories of Gorenstein modules. Our proofs utilize properties of Gorenstein projective objects within these categories of Gorenstein modules. Such an extension of Bass's conjecture could have significant implications for the investigation of Gorenstein projective dimensions within these categories of Gorenstein modules. Furthermore, we employ a different technique to investigate a related conjecture, which can be viewed as a generalization of Bass's conjecture to Golan and Sapir's conjecture, for a category of Gorenstein projective modules. To prove our theorems, we also develop a new approach for a conjecture by M. Auslander, providing an affirmative answer for Gorenstein rings of specific types. Our methodology relies on minimal injective resolutions, a technique that has been increasingly valuable in recent years.

Introduction and Contributions
Modeling network data remains a significant and evolving challenge in statistics, machine learning, and network science. The rising availability of network data, particularly in social and biological contexts, has intensified the demand for effective representation learning techniques. While continuous embedding methods have emerged as a standard for graph and social networks, data derived from finite populations often exhibit unique properties that distinguish them. For instance, discrete, labeled, and embedded finite networks are prevalent, yet their distinct characteristics are often addressed in isolation in existing literature.

In this work, we present a unified, entropy-based framework for representing labeled, embedded finite networks. We relate this method to previous embedding research, demonstrating its capacity to encode various network features and its adaptability to diverse representation learning tasks. Our main contributions are as follows:
1. We propose a unified, entropy-based framework for represented labeled networks.
2. We establish a connection to prior embedding literature, showing the framework's ability to encode diverse network features.
3. We develop a suite of synthetic data and experimental designs to evaluate the framework's performance.
4. We illustrate that synthetic data performance is comparable to, and in some cases superior to, that of state-of-the-art methods.

The structure of this work is as follows:
- Section 2 presents a literature review of graph representation techniques.

efficient utilization of the radio spectrum. While cognitive radio offers a potential solution, significant challenges remain regarding interference management and the development of appropriate radio access mechanisms. This paper presents a novel cognitive radio access method grounded in a fundamental trade-off: the conflict between maintaining low average interference and ensuring adequate data rates for primary users. We introduce a new protocol termed Adaptive Time-Splitting (ATS), designed to dynamically allocate transmission time to secondary users based on channel conditions. ATS operates transparently to the primary network, requiring no prior knowledge of cognitive user characteristics. Through a detailed analytical framework, we demonstrate that the proposed scheme can substantially lower average interference while safeguarding primary users against significant performance degradation. Simulation results validate our analytical findings and indicate that ATS outperforms existing protocols. Furthermore, we examine the impact of varying cognitive radio populations on average interference and show that the ATS-based approach enables a higher number of secondary users to coexist compared to other methods. Finally, we assess the primary network's robustness by evaluating how different durations of spectrum unavailability affect secondary user performance. Our findings reveal that the proposed scheme effectively mitigates the "Joker effect," ensuring that secondary users do not significantly impair primary user performance. In summary, ATS provides a practical and effective framework for cognitive radio access that is transparent to primary networks. The paper includes analytical proofs and simulations supporting these conclusions. While GPDs for valence quarks in the proton are now sufficiently refined to enable analytic modeling, gluon GPDs remain overly uncertain to yield significant insights. To address this, we employ a machine learning approach to derive GPDs for gluons from existing experimental data. Specifically, we utilize a convolution neural network to generate GPDs consistent with both current numerical datasets and their associated uncertainties. Our results indicate that by 2028, data from the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) will constrain the gluon GPD central value within approximately 20%, with uncertainties of similar magnitude; consequently, no significant new information regarding the gluon longitudinal momentum parameter $H$ is anticipated. Furthermore, we predict that in 2028, the data will allow for the determination of the gluon transverse position parameter $\tilde{H}$ with a precision of about 10%. Both GPD parameters exhibit a strong correlation coefficient of approximately 0.8. These findings underscore the critical role of the EIC in elucidating the gluon structure of the nucleon. Additionally, our predictions may be extended to provide insights into the spatial distribution of gluons within individual nucleons inside heavy-ions. Furthermore, we have developed a Python package that integrates machine learning with GPDs, offering a flexible platform for future research. As an example, we use this tool to examine the correlation between GPDs and parton distribution functions. Our future work will concentrate on enhancing the precision of GPDs for gluons using the EIC and other upcoming experiments. These advancements will significantly improve our understanding of the gluon structure of the nucleon, the initial-state parton dynamics of relativistic heavy-ion collisions, and the evolution of the universe in its early stages. This paper presents a novel and general framework for handling heterogeneous data, specifically for classification tasks. The method is built upon a non-asymptotic statistical framework that manages multiple training subsets, each containing a distinct number of outliers. Our theoretical analysis covers the error behavior of both regression and classification models. We first examine the regression problem, where the objective is to estimate a function from noisy data. We demonstrate that under a change of measure on the response variable, the regression function can be reliably estimated using data from subsets with different noise levels and a modified statistical measure. Subsequently, we show that reliable estimation remains feasible even when subsets possess heterogeneous data distributions, such as outliers. Finally, we apply this regression methodology to a robust classification framework, proving that the proposed approach enables robust classification learning. Experimental results confirm that our method surpasses current techniques in achieving reliable classification. These findings indicate that, although our theoretical development is established in the regression domain, it can be extended to support robust classification learning. Furthermore, this approach offers a robust classifier capable of managing multiple training subsets with varying levels of corruption. We demonstrate that utilizing a product measure for classification enables robust learning even when individual subset measures cannot guarantee reliable estimation. These results are validated through numerical experiments. Overall, this study offers a theoretical foundation for robust AI system design in real-world scenarios characterized by heterogeneous data. Additionally, it introduces innovative methodologies and robustness analysis tools that may find applications in other contexts, such as reinforcement learning. As a concrete example, we illustrate how the product measure can be employed to construct robust policy evaluation methods. This enables reliable value function estimation when corruption exists in individual states, even if no specific subset remains clean. These products of measures can serve as robust AI system design tools, ensuring reliable performance across diverse real-world data conditions. By simulating the dynamics of an initial Mott insillator state—characterized by zero onsite and nearest-neighbor interactions—we analyze how such a state evolves within an experimental lattice. Our findings indicate that significant deviations from the predicted dynamics, which assume hopping and interaction energies of $J = U = 4$, arise when the onsite energy is reduced below this value. Specifically, the decay of neighboring correlations is markedly accelerated relative to hopping, while the onsite term remains nearly constant. This behavior is explained by a phase diagram of the initial Mott insulator phase, which reveals a transition to a charge- and spin-density wave phase driven by decreasing onsite energy. This specific phase, where charge and spin order parameters are out of phase, is responsible for the observed rapid decay in correlations. Our results demonstrate the critical influence of the onsite energy term on the dynamics of the initial Mott insulator state. Furthermore, this sensitivity offers a valuable diagnostic tool for assessing the stability of the lattice and its occupants. The study of such systems holds substantial promise for investigating exotic phases of matter, such as spin liquids. Additionally, our findings may extend to other quantum many-body systems, including spin models, fermionic superfluids, and superfluids with competing interactions. The thermalization dynamics of these other phases can be examined in future work. Additionally, our research serves as a proof of concept for the broader application of the initial state sensitivity principle in studying non-equilibrium dynamics. This principle suggests that the evolution of an initial state can yield insights into the equilibrium properties of other states that remain inaccessible through conventional means. This work demonstrates that many-body interactions can be precisely and experimentally characterized through spectral functions derived from momentum- and energy-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Specifically, local moments in transition-metal oxides are shown to induce self-energies that produce a many-gaussian lineshape for momentum-resolved spectral functions. By applying this method to La$_{0.85}$Ca$_{0.15}$MnO$_3$, the study quantifies the energy scale of many-body interactions in this system as 100 meV, a value that aligns with characteristics observed in the high-hallon regime of Mn 3d photoemission spectra. This analysis offers a novel pathway for determining the magnitude of many-body interactions across a wide range of materials. However, units of code are frequently tested with an overreliance on established rules and assumptions, leading to a lack of creativity and the potential failure to identify significant, non-obvious defects. This paper introduces a novel machine learning-based approach to unit testing that automatically generates counter-examples to reveal such defects. The study evaluates six leading large language models (LLMs) for their capacity to reason about code and assess their efficacy as a supplement to traditional testing methods. Results indicate that LLMs can effectively detect bugs within software unit test cases, often matching or surpassing state-of-the-art empirical and symbolic execution techniques in specific scenarios. Furthermore, the research proposes prompt engineering strategies to enhance the performance of LLMs for unit testing, such as providing rich in-context examples and utilizing self-consistency check decoders. Ultimately, this work establishes a new direction for NLP applications in software verification by demonstrating the practical viability of LLMs for exposing hidden defects that other methods may miss. both statistical physics and machine learning. This paper examines a specific model of excursions defined over a positive quadrant small-world graph $T_n$, which we introduce here. We examine a Poisson random field defined on $T_n$, conditioned so that every connected excursions—defined as non-empty sets of visited vertices with no external links to unexcited vertices—consist of exactly two vertices. We demonstrate that as $n \to \infty$, the lengths of these excursions converge in distribution to independent geometric random variables. Consequently, the resulting limit object can be described as a "dot-web": a random rooted tree $T$ where every edge is assigned an independent geometric variable taking values 0 or 1.

Our proof relies on demonstrating that a variant of the random field on $T_n$, featuring exponents $p<q$, similarly converges to a dot-web. By analyzing this weaker model, we establish that the number of trees in the web converge to a Poisson distributed variable with parameter 1, while the expected number of webs containing $2k-2$ vertices converges to a constant $\mu_{k}$. We achieve this by constructing and analyzing a specific coupling between the models on complete graphs that exhibits strong contraction properties.

Furthermore, we show that the limit web-configuration space has a constant probability of being connected, equal to $e^{-2}$. The edges of the webs within the limit configuration space are independently present with probability $e^{-2}$ and absent with probability $1-e^{-2}$. This creates a web configuration space that resembles a random forest grown on top of a tree structure $T$. Finally, we establish that the total number of edges across all the webs in the configuration space converges to a Poisson distribution with parameter $e^{-2}$. These findings suggest that the excursions of this specific "two-point" random field serve as an ideal mechanism for learning random dot-forests buried within a tree-structured image.

Keywords: excursions, random field, small world graph, web configuration space, tree, forest.

Consequently, adjusting for finite tunneling rates offers a viable solution to the primary challenge of unequivocally confirming Majorana modes. Additionally, we find that the alternative proposal by Zazunov et al. remains ineffective due to the inability to rule out bulk states. Finally, our analysis indicates that the proposed bias-sweep protocol can successfully identify Majorana modes without being disrupted by charge redistribution. In summary, these findings suggest that the most promising pathway to confirming Majorana modes involves simultaneously evaluating local quasiparticle excitation and charge properties. Such a protocol can be implemented using a superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) to tune the magnetic flux and a single-electron transistor (SET) to quantify fractional quasiparticle excitations. We also examine two specific cases to illustrate these concepts. First, within a $d$-wave superconductor-based spinless Josephson junction, we show that multiple zero-energy modes coexist with the $2\pi$ fractional charge coexisting with a $1$-phase. Second, in a system utilizing distinct superconductors, we observe that Majorana modes emerge at specific fractional charges, whereas bulk states do not. These examples confirm that simultaneously accessing local excitation and charge degrees of freedom is essential for definitively confirming Majorana modes. We anticipate that this proposal will facilitate the conclusive verification of Majorana modes in upcoming experiments. Additional details regarding the calculation of fractional charges, the interpretation of fractional charge dynamics, and the resolution to previously proposed consistency checks can be found in the Appendix. Our discussion includes considerations of multiple fractional charges, varying fractional charges, distinct fractional charges, and unique zero-energy modes. We also address various issues regarding existing experimental proposals, including finite junction length, multiple zero-energy modes, and unique fractional charges. This comprehensive analysis aims to provide a thorough understanding of the proposed scheme and facilitate future experimental investigations. This extension is characterized by an additional parameter $t \in \mathbb{R}$, where $t=0$ recovers the original model. Our findings indicate that the $t$-parameter significantly impacts the spectral distribution of the resulting random matrix model. For instance, when $n$ and $t$ both approach infinity with $t/(n-1)$ remaining positive and bounded, the limiting spectral distribution corresponds to the semicircle law shifted by $4\sigma^2t^2/\pi$, rather than centering at zero as in the standard case. Furthermore, this shifted distribution exhibits $4\sigma^2t^2 \pi^{-1}$-corruption. To our knowledge, this represents the first identification of such corruption phenomena in Gaussian matrix models. Additionally, our approach introduces a novel technique for analyzing the spectral distributions of random matrices. We also derive asymptotic lower bounds for the smallest absolute eigenvalue for specific well-known random matrix models, including the real and complex Wishart ensembles and the Laguerre ensembles. These findings align with and complement recent asymptotic results by Soshnikov and by Benaych-Georges and Nadon. Notably, our bounds are substantially tighter than previously established general results by Chatterjee and by Chen and Shen, and they apply to a broader range of random matrix models. Finally, we demonstrate a link between our results and the recently discovered "4/3-law" in free probability, which describes the semicircle law shifted by $16\sigma^4\mu_3^2$, where $\mu_3$ denotes the third moment of the weight function. This connection validates the "4/3-law" within a wide array of random matrix models. These discoveries were presented in the author's thesis. The current manuscript incorporates a few new results and demonstrates applications to specific classic random matrix models, such as the Gaussian and Laguerre ensembles. Key theorems include novel estimates for the Hilbert transform of Gaussian measures. We also provide explicit examples of corruption phenomena in these random matrix models and compare our general findings with existing literature. Finally, we reveal a relationship between our "shifted" model and the general concept of the "Gaussian deformation" of a probability measure

In the context of a game where a classifier is fixed but an adversary seeks to exploit it, the concept of universal adversarial perturbations (UAPs) was introduced, which remain effective across various inputs and categories. However, the original UAP remains unknown, and its relationship to classifier-specific adversarial examples remains unclear. This study aims to address these questions by investigating the connection between UAPs and individual classifiers. To achieve this, we introduce Adversarial Regularization, a technique that applies an adversarial constraint during the network's training process. Our findings indicate that training a classifier with Adversarial Regularization yields instances that are easier to generate universal perturbations for, whereas evaluating pre-trained networks is significantly more difficult. Additionally, we demonstrate that the Adversarial Regularization loss adheres to the standard trade-off between accuracy and generalization. The results also reveal that different values of the regularization parameter produce perturbations with distinct properties, such as varying degrees of black-box transferability. Furthermore, we observe that while traditional Data Augmentation improves the classifier's accuracy, it simultaneously degrades its robustness against UAPs. Finally, we show that combining Data Augmentation with Adversarial Regularization can enhance robustness even when training data is limited. This paper addresses the automatic alignment of ontologies, a process used to map ontological entities across different domains by defining correspondences between equivalent entities. Alignments are pivotal for integrating and querying distributed ontological knowledge bases. Given the labor-intensive nature of manually annotating mappings, which restricts current research to a few well-studied ontology pairs, there is a critical need to develop methods that support interactive alignment. While recent studies have focused on predicting alignments between ontologies, research into human-in-the-loop, person-computer collaboration within this field remains limited. This paper advances the understanding of person-computer collaboration in ontology alignment by reporting on an empirical study of 30 participants tasked with aligning two ontologies using a state-of-the-art automated system. The research investigates individual preferences and strategies regarding the order of alignment activities, as well as how participants leverage the system, including a detailed analysis of their suggestions and revisions. The study offers a comprehensive analysis of alignments, suggestions, and revisions alongside a high-level overview of the participants' working styles. Findings highlight that human experts tend to align classes and properties early in the session, even when these elements are not early in the display order, suggesting a strategy of focusing on high-level structures before details. Additionally, the study identifies specific alignment tasks where experts rely more on the automated system, demonstrating a clear distinction between activities where experts trust the system versus those where they prefer manual control. Finally, the research examines how the interface design influences work patterns, revealing that experts often suggest and revise class mappings at higher rates than other mappings, and that the order of interaction with alignment features impacts both the number and quality of alignments produced. Overall, this research deepens the current understanding of person-computer collaboration in ontology alignment and provides valuable insights for future system development. Limitations include the fact that all participants lacked prior experience with the specific interface, and the sample size was small and drawn from a single institution. Future work aims to test these findings on a larger, more diverse group of users, gather data on professional backgrounds and domain expertise, and explore how these factors influence alignment strategies. Furthermore, efforts will be made to integrate this approach into broader development efforts, such as the FLOPO project, to test scalability and address additional challenges. This research contributes to several areas within interactive ontology editing, collaboration, and specific applications in biomedical and life science information management. We computed the phoretic factor, which quantifies the Soret effect, across a spectrum of external body forces. By integrating experimental data on self-diffusion coefficients and partial molecular volumes, we estimated the thermodiffusion coefficient. However, measuring reactions involving highly reactive radical species is difficult due to their short lifespans, forcing researchers to rely on theoretical calculations. This study focuses on the reaction between atomic oxygen and formyl (HCO), a species formed by CO oxidation in interstellar clouds. We compare the results of the present study with a recent study by P. Casali et al. regarding the potential energy surface (PES) and reaction rate for this process. Our findings indicate that the reaction proceeds barrierlessly, yielding CO and H$_2$O, and that the rate is nearly temperature-independent, even at temperatures approaching 0 K. In contrast, the PES and reaction rate reported by Casali et al. suggest a small entrance barrier and a rate significantly lower than our results. The significant discrepancy between our results and those of the previous study is primarily attributed to differences in the treatment of the oxygen atom. Specifically, the CAS-DZ basis set used by Casali et al., which is highly symmetric, fails to adequately describe the oxygen atom, leading to a reaction barrier and influencing the reaction pathway and rate. To ensure reliable calculations of the reaction between O and HCO, it is essential to employ a basis set with low symmetry and optimized orbitals, or alternatively, to use an effective Hamiltonian for the oxygen atom. Furthermore, our calculated rate is approximately two orders of magnitude higher than rates derived from observations, suggesting that the O + HCO reaction is not the mechanism responsible for the deactivation of HCO observed in the interstellar medium. Finally, the O + HCO reaction rate is also substantially lower than rates for O + other radical reactions, such as O + OH and O + HO$_2$, which are considered dominant during CO oxidation in the interstellar medium. This suggests that the O + OH and O + HO$_2$ reactions are not the primary drivers of CO oxidation in these environments. Additionally, our results are significantly lower than O + H$_2$CO and O + CH$_3$ rates but comparable to O + H$_2$S and O + H$_2$SO rates, implying that the O + HCO reaction could be a dominant destruction pathway for HCO in the interstellar medium. $r$-partite graph $F$, denoted $ex(n, F)$, represents the maximum number of edges possible in an $r$-partite graph on $n$ vertices that does not contain $F$ as a subgraph. For a given $r$, the corresponding \emph{Tur\'an graph} $T_{n,r}(F)$ is constructed by removing all edges between nonadjacent parts in $K_r$ and then adding $\lfloor n/r \rfloor$ vertices to each part. When $n$ is divisible by $r$, $T_{n,r}(F)$ is simply the $T_{n,r}$ graph, which consists of $r$ parts where each part forms a clique. The \emph{Tur\'an density} of $F$ is defined as $\pi(F) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{ex(n, F)}{\binom{n}{r-1}}$.

In 1962, Erd\H{o}s, Faudree, Faudree, and Rousseau established that if $F$ is an $r$-partite graph containing at least one edge, then $\pi(F) > 1/2$ whenever $r \geq 4$. Furthermore, we identify the unique graph structure that maximizes $\alpha(T_{n,r}(F))$. conduction theory, termed the Biot-Onsite-Lattice (BOL) approach. This new framework retains the core tenets of the original Biot theory by incorporating thermal relaxation and memory effects, yet it fundamentally diverges from the classical model by integrating two additional mechanisms: molecular vibration and photon emission resulting from electron-phonon interactions. The theory is established through a coupled system of balance laws and constitutive equations derived via the extended state-space approach. To demonstrate its applicability and obtain memory-dependent evolution equations, we employ both integral-transform and state-space methods. Our findings reveal that the model yields purely damped thermal waves and establishes momentum and energy exchange between continuum entities (such as atoms) and their on-site point particles (such as photons or lattice neighbors). The coupling is mediated by the thermal relaxation of electrons, governed by a temperature-dependent nonlinear function of the thermal potential, $\theta(x,t)$. This leads to a memory-dependent heat equation featuring three new parameters, one of which is extremely small, allowing the model to simplify to the extended Surma-Liu theory under specific conditions. The state-space method produces a mixed-order coupled system comprising a third-order heat equation, a second-order evolution equation for the thermal displacement, and a population balance equation for photon density. For linearized versions of both the extended state-space and the integral-transform systems, we derive equivalent forms that differ only by higher-order terms, confirming the consistency of the mathematical frameworks. In a subsequent study, we will present numerical simulations of the nonlinear BOL model and explore its potential to explain high-temperature material behavior and ultrafast laser heating phenomena. Furthermore, our numerical results indicate that VSV achieves superior accuracy and a greater dynamic range compared to other existing protocols. These findings strongly suggest that VSV is well-suited for implementation on near-future noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, including those capable of hybrid classical-quantum computation. In conclusion, VSV represents a robust and accurate tool for detecting quantum correlations and entanglement, with potential applications in quantum phase transitions, thermodynamics, and material science. As NISQ devices advance, VSV is expected to become an essential resource for investigating entanglement within such systems. This work also serves as a NISQ challenge, inviting the quantum community to utilize VSV for exploring quantum thermodynamics, phase transitions, and other related fields. The Python code for VSV is accessible at \url{https://github.com/niqin/VSV}. This study examines how a stationary fast ion distribution, characterized by a finite temperature anisotropy, influences the microtearing stability of toroidally periodic perturbations. Utilizing a local, electrostatic, gyrokinetic framework, we determine the critical temperature anisotropy threshold for the onset of these modes. In a collisionless environment, this threshold corresponds to the anisotropy required for magnetic reconnection; however, collisional effects can either enhance or suppress its magnitude. For magnetized electrons, the critical anisotropy remains independent of collisionality, aligning with large-scale two-fluid reconnection theory. Conversely, in the gyroradius limit, anisotropy dependence varies with the fast ion species: in the collisionless regime, it is negligible, whereas in the collisional limit, it scales with the squared electron-to-ion mass ratio and matches fluid two-reconnection theory predictions. However, current systems typically rely on brief queries, necessitating users to make multiple successive searches to find specific images. This paper introduces a unified framework for visual query continuation, designed to interpret user queries as exploratory actions and suggest subsequent queries based on prior results. The framework is divided into two components: a query interpreter that analyzes a given query to determine its intent, and a suggestion engine that uses the output from the interpreter to propose follow-up queries. We evaluate the framework's performance in providing query continuations across three image search platforms. Our findings indicate that a system leveraging query interpretation can effectively identify the user's search intent, while another system using the same interpreter to generate suggestions can improve the discovery of relevant images. In this work, we introduce a shape optimization approach designed to manipulate the complete geometric structure of a Lorentzian manifold. Our primary objective is to refine the spacetime metric so that it satisfies the Einstein equations while minimizing the $L^2$-norm of the source term. To achieve this, we employ the adjoint method, which necessitates the development of the calculus of variations for a metric constrained by the Einstein equation. This requires defining a suitable tangent space for the metric, interpreting the Einstein equations, and deriving the corresponding linearized system and its associated adjoint equation. Although the resulting variational problem is non-Riemannian, we employ the adjoint variable to regularize the gradient and formulate an optimized metric that approximates the Riemannian manifold corresponding to the Ricci eigenvalue of interest. We establish the existence of solutions and provide a rigorous justification for the gradient calculations. Furthermore, numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can accurately optimize a metric to satisfy specific spectral properties of its Ricci tensor. These experiments also validate the theoretical findings, illustrating notable numerical accuracy. Finally, we discuss potential future extensions of this methodology, particularly for applications in numerical spectral analysis and spectral reconstruction. Through numerical experiments, we confirm that shape optimization serves as an effective gradient-based technique for properties such as spectral reconstruction and spectral analysis. This study thus advances novel algorithms within a broad non-Riemannian setting, offering algorithmic regularizations for regularize-to-solve strategies. These advancements are anticipated to significantly benefit spectral analysis techniques in non-Riemannian geometries. Additionally, our numerical experiments demonstrate that ShapeGradient exhibits remarkable accuracy and robustness, even when input data contains substantial noise. These results are expected to enhance existing numerical spectral analysis methods in non-Riemannian geometries. Moreover, spectral analysis is a critical component of Computer-Aided Design (CAD) in imaging, making this research a novel contribution to CAD in imaging domains. The CAD in imaging community has recently embraced Shape Gradient in imaging for CAD inverse problems, further underscoring the significance of this application. Leveraging this context, we have successfully applied ShapeGradient to specific image imaging CAD problems, yielding promising outcomes. This application of ShapeGradient in imaging CAD further solidifies the efficacy of this technique in imaging CAD contexts. Our future work will involve more extensive experiments within imaging CAD to demonstrate the robustness of Shape optimization and further integrate this methodology into image imaging CAD. This protocol enables multiple uncoordinated stations to achieve full-duplex packet transmission without requiring any synchronization between devices. Leveraging the frequency-dependent nature of WiFi channel impairments, we employ a distributed frequency notification mechanism paired with a novel joint duplex radio design to facilitate simultaneous duplex communication. Additionally, we propose a robust network scheduling mechanism capable of adapting to the highly dynamic channel conditions inherent in unlicensed spectrum. Extensive simulations conducted under various scenarios demonstrate significant performance gains for our protocol, indicating a promising path toward efficient duplex transmission in next-generation WiFi environments. The supplementary material provides detailed derivations for the protocols discussed. Our proposed system is particularly well-suited for WiFi applications requiring duplex transmission under asymmetric channel conditions. Current research is underway to experimentally validate these findings. WiFi, originally conceived for half-duplex transmission, faces performance bottlenecks in duplex scenarios due to the need for fast, reliable, and high-throughput point-to-point connections alongside high network throughput. While our solution is specifically optimized for WiFi, it is also applicable to other wireless technologies. Furthermore, the approach is inherently distributed, making it resilient to the central node failures often encountered in wireless systems. We acknowledge that the 60 GHz band is susceptible to multipath blockage, which can be mitigated through antenna diversity and frequency diversity. Additionally, the system incorporates a mechanism to switch to lower frequencies when necessary. Our solution is designed to coexist with existing single-AP networks featuring both half-duplex and duplex modes. Although our primary focus is on single-AP networks, the proposed system can also be extended to multi-AP networks. Finally, we demonstrate that this approach is applicable to other wireless technologies characterized by asymmetric channels. We also address the issue of interference caused by other devices transmitting on the same frequency and show that this does not significantly impact overall system performance. The paper includes detailed derivations for the protocols under consideration. Our findings indicate that the system is highly energy-efficient, with the duplex radio transmitting simultaneously only when the throughput gain is substantial.
